title: Negative Role of the Receptor-Like Kinase GbMIK2 in Regulating Cotton Verticillium Wilt Resistance.
authors: Cai, Chaowei; Zhu, Jiaxuan; Hu, Shanci; Liu, Qi; Li, Yuzhe; Xu, Dan; Zhang, Tongtong; Ge, Yuting; Wang, Ping; Cheng, Kai; Zhang, Xiangyu; Shang, Baoshuan; Zheng, Huanquan; Liu, Jinggao; Cai, Yingfan; Gu, Aixing; Yi, Feifei; Zhang, Xiao
abstract: The leucine-rich repeat receptor-like kinases (LRR-RLKs) function in multifaceted processes in plant growth, reproduction, cell differentiation and immunity. However, the role of the RLK gene MIK2 (Male discoverer 1-Interacting receptor-like Kinase 2) in regulating cotton resistance to Verticillium dahliae remains unclear. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of GbMIK2 or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knocking out of GhMIK2 increased cotton resistance to V. dahliae infection, while ectopic expression of GbMIK2 in Arabidopsis thaliana decreased the plant resistance, indicating a negative role of GbMIK2 in cotton Verticillium wilt resistance. GbMIK2 interacted with its co-receptor GbBAK1 during V. dahliae infection in the initial immune response, resulting in activation of the MAPK cascade. GbMIK2 interacted in the membrane and nucleus with GbOCP3, which also plays a negative role in Verticillium wilt resistance. Both GbMIK2 and GbOCP3 are located in the membrane and nucleus. Their interaction blocked the reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst and jasmonic acid (JA)-mediated resistance to V. dahliae, resulting in suppression of cotton resistance to Verticillium wilt. These results collectively indicate that GbMIK2, interacting with GbOCP3, acts as a negative regulator in modulating cotton Verticillium wilt resistance, providing new insights to the understanding of mechanisms of RLKs in cotton disease resistance.

title: From immunity to identity to exaptation: RNA-based self/non-self discrimination across cellular life.
authors: Xie, Qiuhua; Ma, Ling; Wang, Ziyi; Duan, Yuange; Cao, Qi
abstract: Distinguishing self from non-self is a universal imperative of life, where such discrimination at RNA level is both evolutionarily rational and urgently required to maintain homeostasis. Across kingdoms, organisms have evolved distinct yet convergent strategies to achieve this goal. Animals broadly employ A-to-I mRNA editing and other modifications as self-tags; plants and fungi mainly rely on RNA interference, spatial segregation, and m(6)A methylation; and prokaryotes utilize CRISPR-Cas immunity as a programmable analog of self-recognition. Despite their efficacy, these systems harbor intrinsic vulnerabilities that viruses might exploit through mimicry and modification theft, perpetuating a dynamic host-pathogen arms race. During evolution, these defense mechanisms might be exapted for new roles in hosts: A-to-I editing diversified proteomes, and m(6)A methylation became a global regulator of mRNA fate. Together, these observations reveal that mechanisms born from conflict might be repurposed to drive molecular innovation, linking self-recognition, adaptation, and the evolution of complexity.

title: PRKAG2 Cardiac Syndrome: A Comprehensive Review of Clinical Manifestations, Pathophysiological Mechanisms, and Precision Medicine Frontiers.
authors: Nogueira, Yzabella Alves Campos; Martins, Mariana Barreto; de Abreu Oliveira, Andre Lacerda; Facanha, Arnoldo Rocha; Sternick, Eduardo Back; Dias, Glauber Monteiro
abstract: PRKAG2 cardiac syndrome (PCS) is a metabolic storage cardiomyopathy caused by pathogenic variants in the PRKAG2 gene encoding the gamma2-subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). It is defined by left ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular preexcitation and progressive conduction system disease accompanied by early-onset atrial arrhythmias. This review systematically evaluates PCS, outlining its clinical manifestations, genotype-phenotype spectrum, and diagnostic clues that distinguish it from sarcomeric hypertrophy. It explores underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, detailing how chronic AMPK activation drives glycogen accumulation via allosteric G6P activation of glycogen synthase, following a biphasic temporal model from early GLUT4-mediated glucose flooding to late metabolic feedback suppression. It further examines how Akt-mTOR hyperactivation fosters hypertrophy and how activated fasciculoventricular pathways mediate preexcitation. Finally, it reviews current supportive clinical management and highlights emerging precision medicine frontiers-including RNA-based silencing, pharmacological pathway inhibitors, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing-that aim to shift PCS care toward targeted disease modification.

title: Light-triggered, one-pot ERA/CRISPR-Cas12a platform with photocleavable crRNA gating for dual-modal Mycoplasma pneumoniae detection.
authors: Zou, Lintao; Wang, Lin; Liang, Mingxing; Peng, XiaoZhen; Li, Yue; Liu, Mengzhao; Deng, Zhongliang
abstract: Closed-tube, one-pot CRISPR diagnostics based on light-triggered crRNA uncaging offer a practical strategy for contamination-free nucleic acid detection, yet buffer incompatibility, reagent costs, and instrument dependence remain limiting factors. Here, we report a light-responsive, dual-modal, one-pot platform that integrates ERA (enzymatic recombinase amplification) with CRISPR-Cas12a for rapid Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) detection. A photocleavable linker-modified blocking strand suppresses Cas12a activity during amplification and releases functional crRNA upon brief UV irradiation, enabling on-demand activation within a sealed tube. A unified buffer was developed to support both ERA and Cas12a activity without compromising either component. Under the specific procurement conditions of this study, the per-reaction reagent cost was USD 3.21 for bulk-purchased ERA reagents, compared with USD 7.47 for RPA reagents. The assay achieves limits of detection of 5 copies/muL by real-time fluorescence and 10 copies/muL by LFA (lateral flow assay). Within this study cohort of 71 clinical nasopharyngeal swab specimens, the fluorescence readout yielded 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity, while the LFA readout achieved 98.0% sensitivity and 100% specificity. This closed-tube, low-cost platform provides a versatile framework for light-triggered one-pot CRISPR diagnostics in decentralized settings.

title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity.
authors: Gupta, Dipika; Ding, Xia; Zhang, Lianglin; Coleman, Kate E; Tang, Grace; Lee, Wei Ting C; Oyer, Jon; Kang, Xiaolin; Ramms, Dana J; Yu, Ziqi; VanArsdale, Todd; Fenyo, David; Huang, Tony T; Rothenberg, Eli
abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4-PARP1-TIMELESS-DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers.

title: A modular lentiviral system for multiplexed gene perturbation and functional analysis suggests interdependence of hormone receptors in breast cancer growth in vivo.
authors: Alam, Seher; Matvienko, Daria; Bostrom, Johan; Pires, Maria J; Papadimitropoulou, Aikaterini; Eshtad, Saeed; Sanjiv, Kumar; Qian, Hong; Valerie, Nicholas Ck; Brisken, Cathrin; Altun, Mikael
abstract: Precise and flexible control of gene expression is essential for dissecting gene function in complex biological systems. Although recent developments in genetic engineering and CRISPR/Cas9 technology have expanded tools for gene activation, suppression, and editing, their application in physiologically relevant models remains challenging, time-consuming, and expensive. Here, we present a modular, doxycycline-inducible vector system that integrates gene overexpression, shRNA-mediated knockdown, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated regulation within a single, lentivirus-compatible system. The modular design allows rapid exchange of selection markers, epitope tags, and reporters via Gateway cloning, providing broad adaptability across experimental settings. In addition to standard fluorescent and luminescent reporters, the system includes advanced sensors, such as Fucci cell cycle reporters, to enable monitoring of cellular processes. By combining fluorescence barcoding with combinatorial genetic perturbations, the platform supports multiplexed analysis of gene function and genetic interactions through phenotypic characterization by fluorescence imaging or flow cytometry. We demonstrate its utility in vivo with breast cancer intraductal xenografts, which suggest that ER+ breast cancer cells (MCF7) rely on androgen, estrogen, and progesterone receptors for in vivo growth. This versatile gene perturbation system provides tight temporal control, streamlined implementation, and high-content phenotyping capacity facilitating efficient in vitro and in vivo studies while reducing the use of animals in in vivo validation experiments. It thus expands the experimental repertoire for dynamic, multigene interrogation in complex systems.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
authors: Nishimura, Takanori; Kunisada, Yuya; Li, Hongmei Lisa; Highfill, Chad A; Nagasawa, Koji; Tsujihata, Yoshiyuki
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

title: AI-enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 therapeutics: Advances in precision, safety, and delivery.
authors: Boretti, Alberto
journal: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

title: mGluR6 is required for cone terminal targeting and synaptic layer assembly during human retinal development.
authors: Bahmani, Leila; Galvan, Patricia; Hosseini, Hirad; Bai, Jinlun; Bharathan, Sumitha P; Chen, Michael; Stepanian, Kayla; Thornton, Matthew E; Grubbs, Brendan H; Nagiel, Aaron
abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 6 (mGluR6), encoded by GRM6, is a core component of the ON-bipolar signaling cascade in the retina, but its role in human retinal development remains unclear. Here, we used temporally controlled CRISPR-based genetic ablation in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived retinal organoids to define the developmental functions of mGluR6. Unexpectedly, we found that mGluR6 is expressed not only in ON-bipolar cells but also transiently in cone photoreceptors during human retinal development, a pattern not observed in the mouse retina. Early loss of GRM6 before synaptogenesis disrupted cone pedicle architecture, leading to mislocalization of synaptic proteins including Bassoon, ELFN2, and TRPM1, and ultimately resulting in widening or duplication of the outer plexiform layer. In contrast, deletion after synapse formation did not alter retinal architecture. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized, temporally restricted role for mGluR6 in cone terminal targeting and synaptic layer assembly during human retinal development.

title: Antigen scaffolds drive preferential expansion of functional genetically engineered CAR and TCR T cells.
authors: Johansen, Kristoffer Haurum; Ramanathan, Keerthana; Rodriguez-Pardo, Carlos; Gjelstrup, Anne Kargaard; Halldorsdottir, Holmfridur Rosa; Voss, Lasse Frank; Tvingsholm, Siri; Grand, Laura Stentoft; Dionisio, Edoardo; Skriver, Alberte H; Frederiksen, Louise Pii; Bjornson, Mette; Svensson-Frej, Marcus; Ormhoj, Maria; Hadrup, Sine Reker
abstract: T cells engineered to express recombinant T cell receptors (TCRs) or chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can induce durable clinical responses in solid and hematological malignancies. However, manufacturing is resource intensive and often yields highly differentiated, exhausted T cell products. To address this, we developed an antigen-scaffold (Ag-scaffold) technology that presents cognate antigen alongside stimulatory cytokines to preferentially expand genetically engineered T cells. We expanded CRISPR-Cas9- and lentivirally engineered TCR T cells with peptide MHC (pMHC)-presenting Ag-scaffolds and anti-CD19 CAR T cells with CD19-presenting Ag-scaffolds. By applying cognate pMHC Ag-scaffolds, we achieved on average 69% (+/-22%) antigen-specific T cells after 14 days of culture with a cytotoxic, proliferative profile. Ag-scaffold expansion enhanced initial TCR and CAR cytotoxicity; repeated rechallenges showed sustained control. In vivo, Ag-scaffold-expanded CRISPR-Cas9-engineered NY-ESO-1-specific TCR T cells and anti-CD19 CAR T cells also showed improved tumor control in lymphoma and solid tumor xenograft models compared to cells expanded with IL2/7/15.

title: A VIPR that wraps: A triplex biochemistry for next-gen biotechnology.
authors: Xu, Lingjie; Bao, Zehua
abstract: A putative ancestor to CRISPR systems, VIPR, was recently discovered.(1)(,)(2) VIPR adopts a distinct non-contiguous code for PAM-free RNA-guided DNA recognition and is ultracompact and reprogrammable, making it a promising candidate for various genome-manipulation applications. Many open questions remain and their answers will foster exciting opportunities for next-generation biotechnology.

title: Editing of SpNRAMP3, SpCAX3, and SpHMA3 differentially affects cadmium concentrations and growth responses in Sedum plumbizincicola.
authors: Wu, Xiaotong; Zhang, Yixin; Mo, Yanlan; Liu, Huan; Wu, Longhua; Ren, Hongxu; Zhang, Yaping; Xu, Wenzhong
abstract: Sedum plumbizincicola is a Cd/Zn hyperaccumulator with exceptional Cd tolerance and shoot accumulation capacity. Here, bioinformatic analysis, subcellular localization, heterologous expression in yeast, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing were combined to characterize the role of SpNRAMP3 in Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation and its functional relationships with SpCAX3 and SpHMA3. SpNRAMP3 encodes a protein with 11 predicted transmembrane domains and shows a localization pattern consistent with tonoplast association; it is expressed in roots, stems and leaves and displays Cd-responsive expression. Heterologous expression of SpNRAMP3 in yeast increased cellular Cd accumulation and conferred Cd hypersensitivity. Two independent SpNRAMP3-edited lines showed greater Cd sensitivity and lower Cd concentrations in young leaves, supporting a role for SpNRAMP3 in Cd homeostasis, growth response, and tissue Cd allocation. Heterologous expression of SpCAX3 also altered cellular Cd accumulation and Cd sensitivity in yeast. Compared with the wild type, the spnramp3spcax3 double-edited lines showed 72.5-79.8% lower Cd concentrations in young leaves and reduced relative growth inhibition under Cd stress, whereas the spnramp3sphma3 lines showed 28.2-58.6% lower Cd concentrations in young leaves but substantially greater growth inhibition. These results suggest that SpHMA3 primarily mediates vacuolar Cd sequestration, whereas SpNRAMP3 and SpCAX3 may contribute to Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation through distinct but functionally connected processes. These proteins may act together to support Cd hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance in S. plumbizincicola. This study provides a framework for understanding Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation in hyperaccumulator plants and identifies candidate targets for genome-editing-based improvement of phytoremediation.

title: IL-15/IL-15Ralpha-targeted CRISPRa boosts NK cell effector function against HIV-infected cells.
authors: Brancazio, Samuel; Burdo, Tricia H; Shan, Liang; Kaminski, Rafal
abstract: Like many other immune cell types, natural killer (NK) cells exhibit impaired functionality in people with HIV (PWH), limiting their ability to efficiently target and eliminate HIV-infected cells and contributing to the persistence of the HIV reservoir. Recently, adoptive NK cell therapy using activated or engineered NK cells has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer; however, its application to HIV remains in the early stages of development. NK cells primarily rely on interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling for their development, survival, and maintenance, and dysregulated IL-15 signaling has been reported in PWH. We hypothesized that simultaneous enhancement of IL-15 and IL-15 receptor alpha (IL-15Ralpha) expression would improve NK cell effector function and promote clearance of HIV reservoir. Utilizing dCas9-VPR-mediated multiplex CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), we successfully upregulated both IL-15 and IL-15Ralpha expression in the same primary NK cells without altering the genomic sequence. CRISPRa-treated NK cells displayed increased IL-15 and IL-15Ralpha transcript levels, as measured by RT-qPCR and significantly elevated surface expression of IL-15Ralpha, as determined by flow cytometry. Enhanced IL-15/IL-15Ralpha expression increased NK cell metabolic activity and cytotoxicity against target K562 cells, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line, indicating improved effector function. Furthermore, in co-culture experiments using an HIV-positive T-cell line, IL-15/IL-15Ralpha-CRISPRa-treated NK cells demonstrated enhanced target cell elimination and increased secretion of IFN-gamma. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept that multiplex CRISPRa can be used to enhance NK cell function, representing a novel strategy to improve persistence and therapeutic efficacy in HIV and other disease settings.

title: An Anther-Specific Sugar Transporter SlSTP9 Is Modulated by SlDof12 to Regulate Anther Elongation and Reproductive Success in Tomato.
authors: Wang, Xingyi; Li, Shihui; Liu, Zijian; Liang, Meiting; Tang, Yuxi; Li, Xin; Gao, Lihong; Tian, Yongqiang; Ma, Si
abstract: Successful pollination in crops relies on the intricate coordination between the anther and the style. However, the role of sugar transporters in modulating floral architecture and influencing pollination success remains poorly understood. This study investigates the function and transcriptional regulation of the tomato sugar transporter, SlSTP9, using a combination of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing, yeast functional complementation, microscale thermophoresis, transcriptomic, and metabolic profiling. We identify SlSTP9 as an anther endothecium/middle-layer-specific sugar transporter localized to the plasma membrane. Loss of SlSTP9 function results in impaired endothecium and middle-layer cell expansion, leading to shortened anthers, premature dehiscence, stigma exsertion, and ultimately pollination failure. In contrast, overexpression of SlSTP9 enhances fruit set. Functional assays show that SlSTP9 exhibits high affinity for fructose and galactose, and its loss in the slstp9 mutant leads to excessive accumulation of galactose, activation of phenylpropanoid metabolism, and premature lignification of endothecium cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Dof-family transcription factor SlDof12, which is also localized in the anther endothecium and middle layer, directly represses SlSTP9 expression. Overexpression of SlDof12 recapitulates the floral defects observed in the slstp9 mutant. These findings reveal a regulatory module involving SlDof12 and SlSTP9 that controls anther elongation by preventing premature lignification, highlighting a novel role for sugar transporters in shaping floral architecture and modulating reproductive success.

title: A GmGTF3A-GmSTF1/2 module governs GmPsbS-dependent photoprotection under high-light stress in soybean.
authors: Lin, Faming; Cao, Junjiao; Yang, Shaolong; Zhao, Chenhao; Fan, Puqing; Xu, Yilei; Wang, Xiaoran; Wang, Ran
abstract: Non-photochemical quenching (NPQ) dissipates excess light energy as heat, preventing photosystem damage. PsbS is essential for energy-dependent quenching (qE), but its transcriptional regulation in crops remains unclear. Here, we characterize the functional roles of two PsbS paralogs in soybean and identify a transcriptional regulatory module that governs their expression under high-light stress. We show that GmPsbS1 and GmPsbS2 are predominantly expressed in leaves, exhibit diurnal rhythms, and encode chloroplast-localized proteins. The CRISPR/Cas9-generated double mutant showed strong photoinhibition under high light, with reduced Pn, impaired NPQ, lower photosystem protein levels, higher ROS accumulation, and greater oxidative damage. Using yeast one-hybrid screening, we identified the bZIP transcription factor GmSTF1 as a direct activator of both GmPsbS genes. GmSTF1/2 activate their respective transcriptional expression by directly binding to the TGACGT cis-element located within their promoter regions, and overexpression of GmSTF1 in soybean enhances NPQ, mitigates oxidative stress, and confers improved tolerance to high-light stress. Furthermore, the C2H2 zinc finger protein GmGTF3A physically interacts with GmSTF1/2 and enhances their transcriptional activation of GmPsbS in transient assays, suggesting that it may function as a putative transcriptional co-activator. Collectively, our findings establish GmPsbS as a key photoprotective executor in soybean, with GmSTF1/2 and GmGTF3A cooperatively activating its expression to fine-tune NPQ under high-light stress, offering insights and targets for improving photosynthetic resilience.

title: COP1 proteins integrate light signaling to fruit plastid development via the HY5-GLK2 module in tomato.
authors: Zhang, Chunli; Tong, Boqin; Wu, Baoguo; Liu, Yue; Wu, Yujie; Xu, Shiqi; Zha, Feier; Liu, Xiangshuai; Wang, Taotao; Wang, Xin; Zhang, Junhong; Dong, Huaxi; Yang, Guoqian; Zhu, Changan; Wang, Yikui; Lin, Li; Yu, Jingquan; Yin, Ruohe
abstract: Light signaling regulates plant development, yet how it differentially controls plastid development across organs remains unclear. Here, we show that two tomato COP1 proteins restrict plastid development in fruits but not in leaves. With CRISPR-Cas9 mutants, we demonstrate that SlCOP1s repress photomorphogenesis by destabilizing SlHY5 and controlling large-scale light-responsive transcription in seedlings. In fruits, SlCOP1s suppress chloroplast development and chlorophyll accumulation by inhibiting SlHY5-dependent activation of GLK2, a key regulator of plastid biogenesis. SlHY5 directly binds the GLK2 promoter and activates its expression in fruits, but not in leaves, highlighting tissue-specific deployment of the SlCOP1-SlHY5 module. This pathway is distinct from CUL4-DDB1-DET1-mediated regulation of GLK stability, indicating multilayered control of GLK2. Enhanced plastid development in Slcop1 double mutants is associated with increased carotenoid accumulation in fruit. Together, these findings uncover a SlCOP1-SlHY5-GLK2 module that links light signaling to fruit plastid development and illustrate how conserved pathways are rewired to control organelle development in a tissue-dependent manner.

title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation.
authors: Chaudhary, Vidyanath; Du, Yong; Mishra, Bikash; Ah Kioon, Marie Dominique; Ahuja, Palak; Ivashkiv, Lionel B; Truchetet, Marie-Elise; Spiera, Robert F; Lakin, Kimberly; Gordon, Jessica K; Barrat, Franck J
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ-TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.

title: PIP5K isoforms and phosphoinositide molecular species in EGF-stimulated PIP3 synthesis: A multi-method approach using enzyme genetic suppression and chemical inhibition in MCF10A cells.
authors: Alexandrou, Iosif; Flemington, Vikki; Swarbrick, Martin E; Cosulich, Sabina; Hawkins, Phillip T; Stephens, Len R
abstract: The membrane phospholipid PI(4,5)P2 has structural functions and is a substrate for PLC and PI3K enzymes to generate Ins(1,4,5)P3, DAG and PI(3,4,5)P3 signals. PIP5Ks, that 5-phosphorylate PI4P, are the major source of PI(4,5)P2 in mammalian cells. Current thinking suggests distinct pools of PI(4,5)P2 may be differentially generated by PIP5Kalpha, beta and gamma isoforms and involved in different physiological functions. Phosphoinositides are comprised of families of acyl-chain variants but are uniquely enriched in C38:4 species. There is evidence that PIP5Ks are selective for certain acyl chain species of PI(4)P. We aimed to understand how inhibition of PIP5Ks impacts PIP3 production and whether they differentially support synthesis of a pool of PI(4,5)P2, that may be marked by a distinct profile of molecular species variants, which supply class I PI3Ks in a non-transformed human cell line (MCF10A cells). Using a combination of siRNA, Cas9/CRISPR-mediated gene knockout (k/o), recently derived selective, small-molecule inhibitors of PIP5Ks and mass-spectrometry-based lipidomic techniques, we attempted to address these questions. We found that MCF10A cells only express PIP5Kalpha and gamma and that neither siRNA-mediated reduction nor k/o of either protein changed the levels or acyl chain profiles of any of the phosphoinositides in Epidermal Growth Factor- (EGF) stimulated MCF10A cells. We found that selective PIP5K inhibition reduced levels of PIP2 and EGF-stimulated PIP3 and increased levels of PIP, however, the acyl-chain-profiles of none of these lipids were significantly altered in MCF10A cells. We found EGF-stimulated Akt, EGF Receptor (EGFR) and MAPK phosphorylation were also reduced by PIP5K inhibitors in this cell line. To deconvolute these results, we tested the impact of a selective PI3Kalpha inhibitor (A66) and found it inhibited PIP3 accumulation and Akt phosphorylation and reduced MAPK phosphorylation but was without effect on total EGFR or its phosphorylation, suggesting some cross-talk between EGF-stimulated activation of class I PI3K and MAPKs in MCF10A cells.

title: The small protein PhrS-P, encoded by the dual-function small RNA PhrS, augments fitness of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the presence of aminoglycosides.
authors: Lilic, Branislav; Cianciulli Sesso, Anastasia; Berghoff, Bork; Moll, Isabella; Sonnleitner, Elisabeth; Blasi, Udo
abstract: PhrS (Pseudomonas Hfq-binding RNA S) is a dual-function small RNA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The base-pairing small regulatory RNA PhrS-R positively regulates pyocyanin biosynthesis. PhrS-R stimulates the production of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) by indirectly activating the translation of pqsR mRNA, encoding the quorum sensing regulator PqsR (MvfR), and by inhibiting the synthesis of the anthranilate degradation regulator AntR. Furthermore, PhrS-R was shown to promote biofilm formation, swarming motility and CRISPR-Cas immunity. In addition, PhrS encodes a 37 amino acid long and conserved small protein (PhrS-P), the function of which remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that PhrS-P is an inner membrane protein which does not contribute to the known physiological roles of its RNA counterpart. RNA-Seq-based transcriptome analyses revealed that multiple aminoglycoside resistance genes, including those of the AmgR regulon, are differentially expressed depending on PhrS-P. AmgR is the response regulator of the AmgRS two-component system (TCS), which affects aminoglycoside and zinc resistance in P. aeruginosa. A PhrS-P-deficient mutant strain exhibited reduced fitness when exposed to sub-inhibitory concentrations of the aminoglycosides tobramycin and amikacin as well as zinc. Based on our findings, we present a working model wherein PhrS-P positively regulates the AmgRS TCS activity through an unknown mechanism, leading to increased bacterial fitness in the presence of aminoglycosides.

title: IDO1 methylation by EZH2 confers resistance to its targeted therapy in colorectal cancer through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic rewiring.
authors: Tang, Yuanjun; Huang, Zhanya; Jia, Yiting; Guo, Yunyun; Cao, Xuedi; Jin, Renjing; Yin, Qianqian; Song, Jiagui; Chen, Huiguang; Zhang, Xintong; Zhou, Xin; Cheng, Rui; Yang, Jianling; Guo, Zhengyang; Bu, Pengcheng; Xue, Lixiang
abstract: Deciphering cancer metabolic reprogramming mechanisms can identify new targets to potentiate EZH2 inhibitor efficacy. Using an in vivo genome-wide CRISPR loss-of-function screen in a CRC mouse model, we pinpointed IDO1 as a key mediator of EZH2 inhibitor resistance. EZH2 blockade remodeled CRC cell metabolism by upregulating IDO1 protein and hyperactivating the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway. Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of IDO1 suppressed tumor growth and rescued EZH2 inhibitor resistance in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, EZH2 directly binds and methylates IDO1. Methylation of IDO1 facilitates IDO1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Accordingly, EZH2 inhibition stabilizes IDO1, augments tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic flux, and ultimately confers therapeutic resistance. In summary, our study identifies IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 methyltransferase activity and validates that disrupting IDO1-mediated tryptophan metabolism is a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 targeted therapy resistance in cancers.

title: PCR-amplified blaKPC-2-triggered Cas12a activation coupled with DNA cube-confined Fc reporter cleavage on a Ti(3)C(2)/CsPbBr(3)@PDA@Au/GCE dual-mode ECL/SERS interface.
authors: Chen, Yijin; Huang, Jiangbin; Wen, Lusheng; Zhu, Qigan; Liu, Jinfa; Meng, Jiarong; Yu, Le
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: Rapid and reliable detection of antibiotic resistance genes is essential for guiding antimicrobial therapy and controlling the spread of carbapenem-resistant pathogens. Herein, we developed a PCR amplicon-activated CRISPR/Cas12a-regulated dual-mode electrochemiluminescence/surface-enhanced Raman scattering biosensor for sensitive detection of the blaKPC-2 resistance gene. A specific blaKPC-2 fragment containing the selected TTTG PAM region was amplified by PCR and used as a double-stranded DNA activator for the crRNA/Cas12a complex. After target recognition, activated Cas12a cleaved the Fc-labeled reporter segments integrated into a DNA cube scaffold assembled on the Ti(3)C(2)/CsPbBr(3)@PDA@Au nanocomposite interface. In the initial state, Fc was positioned close to the Ti(3)C(2)/CsPbBr(3)@PDA@Au-modified GCE surface, resulting in ECL quenching and strong SERS emission. Upon Cas12a-mediated cleavage of the exposed ssDNA reporter segments, Fc-containing fragments were released from the interface, leading to ECL recovery and SERS attenuation. Therefore, the target-induced process enabled an anti-correlated ECL-on/SERS-off signal conversion, and the ratiometric value R = I(ECL)/I(SERS) was used for quantitative analysis. The concentration-dependent response was empirically fitted over 10-10(7) copies per microL, whereas the 10(8) copies per microL group exhibited upper-range response compression. Boundary back-calculation indicated that further quantitative validation is required. Blank-response inverse prediction gave a model-dependent response-equivalent concentration of approximately 1.06 copies per microL; Poisson sampling gave a 95% molecular-sampling threshold of approximately 3.0 copies per microL for a 1.0 microL input. Neither descriptor is an experimentally determined detection or quantification limit. The platform also exhibited good selectivity against other resistance genes and non-target bacterial genomic DNA, together with satisfactory repeatability, reproducibility, stability, and acceptable spike-recovery performance in 10% diluted serum as a model biological matrix, providing preliminary evidence of matrix tolerance rather than clinical validation. This work provides a self-calibrated dual-mode strategy for antibiotic resistance gene detection, while further validation using bacterial lysates, extracted bacterial genomic DNA, and clinical bacterial isolates is required before diagnostic application. qPCR supported linear amplification over 10-10(7) copies per microL; endpoint responses remained observable through 10(8) copies per microL, where quantitative resolution was reduced.

title: CRISPR-Cas Assays for Protein Detection: Strategies and Clinical Applications.
authors: Dong, Shaokun; Zhao, Shuai; Deng, Jinqi; Zhang, Liqin; Sun, Jiashu
abstract: Measurement of protein biomarkers with high accuracy is critical for disease diagnostics and prognostic monitoring. However, conventional analytical platforms for protein detection suffer from insufficient sensitivity for low-abundance targets and require time-consuming, multi-step workflows. The CRISPR-Cas system is emerging as a powerful tool for protein analysis, with advantages including high programmability, excellent sensitivity, and compatibility with diverse readouts. This review presents a systematic overview of recent advances in CRISPR-based protein assays. We first summarize the design principles of aptamer-, antibody-, and enzyme-mediated systems that convert protein recognition events into CRISPR-activatable nucleic acid signals. We next examine the signal amplification and readout strategies, such as direct CRISPR activation, enzyme-mediated nucleic acid amplification, and enzyme-free DNA nanotechnology, along with colorimetric, fluorescent, or electrochemical signal outputs. We also review applications of these assays in infectious diseases, cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we discuss challenges and perspectives for next-generation CRISPR-based protein detection platforms in clinical translation.

title: Correction: Antimicrobial peptides in the era of resistance: integrating AI-driven design, host-microbe interactions, and nanotechnological delivery.
abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.3389/fmicb.2026.1946449.].

title: Inhaled Nanomedicines for Lung Diseases and Injuries: Pharmacological Advances and Clinical Translation.
authors: Kamra, Kajal; Gaur, Sonal; Singh, Jaswinder
abstract: Respiratory diseases remain major causes of morbidity and mortality; however, inadequate pulmonary drug exposure and systemic toxicity continue to limit treatment efficacy. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities for localized, sustained, and targeted therapy. This review examines how disease biology informs pulmonary delivery design across pulmonary fibrosis, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary infections, and acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. It outlines anatomical and biological barriers and compares liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric and hybrid systems, biomimetic carriers, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Particular attention is given to matching therapeutic cargo and carrier properties to fibroblasts, macrophages, tumor cells, and alveolar type II cells. Emerging approaches include mRNA delivery, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR-based editing, alongside alveolar regeneration and biomarker-guided treatment. These strategies are evaluated in relation to their delivery requirements and stage of development. The review also addresses aerosol-device compatibility, manufacturing, repeated-dose safety, regulatory considerations, and clinical outcomes. By connecting delivery mechanisms with disease-specific applications and clinical evidence, this review identifies both therapeutic opportunities and barriers to translation. This integrated perspective can guide the development of inhaled nanomedicines with more reproducible pulmonary delivery, improved treatment efficacy, and acceptable safety.

title: Genomic and clinical factors associated with drug-resistant tuberculosis.
authors: Sundaram, Karthikeyan; Rathinam, Sridhar; Bethunaickan, Ramalingam; Ranganathan, Uma Devi; Dhanapal, Madhavan; Prabhu, Venkataraman
abstract: BACKGROUND: Drug-resistant tuberculosis is a significant global health issue caused by mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the infectious agent of the disease. WHO's End TB Strategy mandates drug susceptibility testing for rifampicin in all confirmed tuberculosis cases and fluoroquinolone testing for rifampicin-resistant cases. OBJECTIVE: The review aims to analyse Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome mutations; Clinical factors linked to drug resistance. Major thematic findings: The mutant otsB1 trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase shows rifampicin resistance in hypoxic conditions. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 is vital for RNI resistance, host cell death, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth. Individuals with drug-susceptible tuberculosis showed higher plasma levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase. NO and iNOS expression can be influenced by factors other than mycobacterial infection. Activated macrophages convert L-arginine to NO via TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma. Serum L-arginine levels were measured in individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and healthy controls. PPE51, PE15, and PE20 improve drug resistance by transporting metal ions and absorbing nutrients. In diagnosis, the CRISPR-guided mutagenic DNA polymerase identifies changes in drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterium smegmatis, recognized for its rapid growth, and the slow-growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis were evaluated using CRISPR-guided DNA polymerase. Also, machine learning and whole-genome sequencing predicted isoniazid, Rifampicin, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis with 90% precision. The BDQ DILI network can offer valuable support on monitor the adverse events of the Anti-tuberculosis therapy. CONCLUSION: Whole genome sequencing, tNGS, and deletion-targeted multiplex PCR effectively detect mutations. Studying PE/PPE genes offers a key chance to drug-resistant tuberculosis research and improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes.

title: CRISPR diagnostics for maternal-infant HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis care: clinical roles and translational gaps.
authors: Luo, Hongzhi; Lin, Lanke; Luo, Fukang; Huang, Xiaoxue; Yu, Qiujie; Li, Qianyi; Zha, He
abstract: This review asked which maternal-infant clinical decisions are plausible targets for CRISPR diagnostics, what evidence currently supports those roles, and what validation remains necessary. We conducted a structured narrative review of CRISPR diagnostics for HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), and syphilis, evaluating complete specimen-to-result systems rather than isolated nuclease reactions. Across the studies identified, HIV early infant diagnosis (EID) had the strongest near-term clinical rationale but lacked validation of microvolume whole blood or dried blood spots, broad HIV-1 inclusivity, and integrated process controls. Maternal HBV had the broadest clinical-specimen evidence, but no identified study established IU/mL-traceable classification around a pregnancy prophylaxis decision boundary. Syphilis direct detection supported a narrower specimen- and stage-dependent adjunctive role and could not replace antenatal serology or exclude congenital infection when negative. Major cross-cutting gaps included specimen preparation, calibration, contamination containment, invalid-result detection, and multisite intended-use validation. These findings do not establish routine clinical readiness. As an evidence-informed development priority, a shared service platform with separately validated pathogen-specific assays appears more defensible in the near term than a universal single-tube triplex.

title: CRISPR-integrated nanobiosensors for rapid and ultra-sensitive food allergen detection: a comprehensive review.
authors: Malitha, Md Dipu; Jain, Harshita; Wolobah, Zayzay; Munzeiwa, Wisdom Archford; Singh, Lovepreet; Sharma, Narendra Kumar
abstract: Reliable allergen detection in increasingly complex and globally distributed food systems demands analytical platforms that overcome the limitations of ELISA, PCR, and traditional biosensors. CRISPR-based diagnostics provide exceptional specificity and programmability, yet their practical performance depends heavily on signal amplification efficiency, enzyme stability, and tolerance to inhibitors commonly present in processed food matrices. Integrating nanomaterials with CRISPR systems offers powerful enhancements in sensitivity, kinetics, and matrix robustness, but a unified evaluation of this convergence is still lacking. This review critically examines CRISPR-nanotechnology-enabled allergen detection by integrating insights on biomarker selection, Cas enzyme architectures, nanomaterial-mediated signal engineering, and emerging device formats including microfluidics, lateral flow assays, and smartphone-based platforms. Persistent challenges such as quantification, multiplexing, reagent stability, and regulatory validation are highlighted. By mapping these technological dependencies and bottlenecks, this review provides a clear roadmap for advancing CRISPR-integrated nanobiosensors toward rapid, ultra-sensitive, and field-deployable allergen monitoring solutions. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10068-026-02206-9.

title: Programming plant resilience with CRISPR/dCas9 epigenome editing: from proof of concept to crop deployment.
authors: Wu, Jacob
abstract: Accelerating climate change is driving unprecedented increases in the frequency and severity of abiotic stresses, threatening global food security and demanding new strategies for crop resilience. Plants have evolved a sophisticated molecular response to recurrent stress through epigenetic priming, where prior exposure induces chromatin-level alterations encoded through DNA methylation, histone modifications, and small RNA pathways. These imprints can persist somatically across cell divisions and, in some cases, be transmitted to subsequent generations. CRISPR/dCas9-based epigenome editing provides the means to install, modify, or erase these same marks at defined loci without altering the underlying sequence. This mini review provides an evidence-based survey of plant dCas9 epigenome editing, distinguishing what each effector class has actually been demonstrated to achieve in planta from what has been shown only in mammalian systems or remains inferred. I map the translational barriers between Arabidopsis proof-of-concept and crop deployment, survey what has been achieved in rice, maize, and tomato, organize the toolkit around the distinct memory logics (type I persistent versus type II poised) it must serve, and identify the priorities that would advance the field from demonstrated single-locus edits toward heritable, deployable modifications. By separating demonstrated capability from extrapolation, this synthesis provides a realistic basis for applying epigenome editing to sustainable agriculture and climate-resilient crop production.

title: An IoT-enabled hybrid paper/polymer-based microfluidic device for rapid detection of Campylobacter jejuni in foods.
authors: He, Yihan; Liu, Jinxin; Li, Shenmiao; Zhao, Xin; Lu, Xiaonan
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is the leading bacterial cause of foodborne gastroenteritis worldwide and represents a major public health concern. We report an IoT-enabled hybrid paper/polymer-based microfluidic device for rapid detection of C. jejuni in food matrices. This platform integrates recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), CRISPR/Cas12a-based sequence recognition, and lateral flow readout within a foldable paper-based architecture incorporating PDMS reservoirs. An IoT workflow was established to enable automated image capture, result classification, and centralized data transmission. Analytical performance was evaluated using both pure cultures and food samples. This assay specifically detected C. jejuni with no observed cross-reactivity among the tested strains and achieved a limit of detection of 5800 CFU mL(-1) using the developed microfluidic device. In chicken breast samples, C. jejuni was reliably detected at initial inoculation levels of 10(0) to 10(3) CFU g(-1) following 6-12 h of enrichment, while higher contamination levels (>10(3) CFU g(-1)) were detectable without enrichment. The complete workflow from DNA extraction to visual readout was completed in  approximately 1 h. By integrating microfluidic sensing, automated data interpretation, and IoT-enabled connectivity, this platform provides a practical and scalable approach for decentralized screening and rapid monitoring of C. jejuni in agri-food system.

title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Galpha(o1) (K278del) mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.
authors: Saez Gonzalez, Maria; Kloosterhuis, Kes; Vreijling, Jeroen; Mei, Hailiang; Hellings, Tom P; Pirolli, Davide; Stam, Anine H; van den Maagdenberg, Arn M J M; Heine, Vivi M; Frimat, Jean-Philippe; van de Pol, Laura A; Baas, Frank; Mikkers, Harald M M
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Galpha(o1) (K278del) variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder. METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Galpha(o1) (K278del) and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed. RESULTS: Galpha(o1) (K278del) mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Galpha(o1) (K278del) variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients. SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

title: RPA-CRISPR/Cas12-based rapid visual on-site detection method for bovine Cryptosporidium.
authors: Liu, Hao; Zhang, Yanmin; Wen, Haifeng; Lu, Jing; Gao, Wa; Wang, Wenlong
abstract: BACKGROUND: Four types of Cryptosporidium (C. parvum, C. bovis, C. ryanae, and C. andersoni) and mixed infections were common among cattle in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region of China, causing severe harm. For grassroots farms and pastures, the prevention and control of bovine Cryptosporidium requires simultaneous detection of the four major Cryptosporidium species, and a one-time diagnosis of bovine Cryptosporidium without distinguishing between species is necessary to achieve more efficient prevention and treatment. In this study, recombinant polymerase amplification (RPA) was combined with the CRISPR/Cas system to design crRNAs and screen RPA primers targeting the 18S rRNA genes of four bovine Cryptosporidium species that primarily infect cattle. RESULTS: Detection results were presented using two distinct single-stranded DNA reporter molecules via fluorescence quantification and lateral flow immunochromatography assay (LFIA) test strips. Using specificity and sensitivity assessments on clinical samples, the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12 visual on-site rapid detection method for bovine Cryptosporidium established in this study was completed within 60 min, with a minimum detection limit of 0.1 copies/microL. There was no cross-reactivity with the six pathogens: Haemonchus contortus, coccidia, Cysticercus tenuicollis, trematode, Caenorhabditis elegans, and tapeworm. Four types of bovine Cryptosporidium were specifically detected. CONCLUSION: Clinical detection showed an 86% positivity rate for bovine Cryptosporidium, consistent with the Cryptosporidium nested PCR method (National Standard). Therefore, the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a rapid on-site detection method established in this study has high specificity and sensitivity, convenience, and speed, without requiring specialized operational steps or expensive equipment.

title: Pangenome analyses reveal divergence and extensive introgression in two global corn pests.
authors: Peng, Yan; Zhang, Yubo; Mao, Kaikai; Zhang, Zhuting; Zhang, Lei; Zhu, Jingyun; Liu, Xinye; Zhao, Chongjun; Fan, Wenmin; Yesaya, Alexander; Wang, Hongru; Heckel, David G; Dopman, Erik B; Zhang, Wei; Xiao, Yutao
abstract: BACKGROUND: Introgression between closely related species can profoundly influence evolutionary trajectories, yet how genomic divergence interacts with introgression, especially in invasive hybridization, remains insufficiently understood. Structural variants (SVs), particularly chromosomal inversions, are key contributors to divergence and may modulate patterns of gene flow. The Asian corn borer (ACB) and European corn borer (ECB), two globally important agricultural pests, provide an excellent system to investigate these processes. RESULTS: We construct a graph-based pangenome from 23 high-quality genome assemblies to characterize genome-wide SVs and introgression between ACB and ECB. We identify over 216,000 SVs, most of which are associated with transposable elements and contribute to interspecific divergence. Population genomic analyses reveal widespread yet asymmetric introgression, predominantly from ACB into ECB populations in China. Introgressed regions are more prevalent in autosomes than in sex chromosomes and are enriched for genes involved in adaptive pathways. In contrast, large inversion regions on the Z chromosome exhibit strong genetic differentiation and reduced introgression, suggesting a role in maintaining species barriers. Notably, a highly divergent region containing the circadian clock gene period (per) shows signatures of selection. Functional validation using CRISPR/Cas9 demonstrates that per significantly influences diapause regulation, linking genomic divergence to adaptive phenotypic variation. CONCLUSIONS: Our results demonstrate that introgression and structural variation jointly shape genomic divergence in these species. While introgression facilitates the spread of adaptive variation, chromosomal inversions restrict gene flow and maintain species integrity. This study provides new insights into the evolutionary mechanisms underlying divergence, adaptation, and invasion in major agricultural pests.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 Rnps Into Cells.
authors: Rajeshwar, V; Kumar, Konda Ravi; Kumar, Gollapalli Rajeev; Roja, Pathakota; Mohan, Vasanth Kumar; Aparna, T Naga
abstract: The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPRassociated protein 9 (Cas9) system has revolutionized genome editing through its precision, simplicity, and programmability. The clinical translation of CRISPR/Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains constrained by major delivery challenges, including large molecular size, instability in biological fluids, and limited cellular penetration. Nanoparticle-mediated, non-viral delivery systems have emerged as a compelling strategy to overcome these barriers by providing targeted, transient, and biocompatible transport of Cas9 RNPs into cells. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in lipid-based, polymeric, peptide, and exosome-derived nanocarriers, focusing on their design principles, mechanisms of uptake, and endosomal escape strategies. Particular attention is given to receptor-mediated targeting, intracellular trafficking, and the emerging translation of lipid nanoparticle systems such as NTLA-2001, which exemplify clinical progress in genome editing. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist. Nanoparticle systems exhibit trade-offs between efficiency, biocompatibility, and scalability. For example, lipid nanoparticles may trigger anti- PEG immune reactions, exosome production faces manufacturing constraints, and polymeric systems risk cytotoxicity or limited degradability. Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 proteins and unpredictable immune responses to nanoparticle components remain significant translational hurdles. By integrating current preclinical and early clinical evidence, this review highlights both the promise and the limitations of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 RNP delivery. Understanding these biological, immunological, and engineering challenges will be crucial for developing safe, efficient, and clinically scalable genome editing platforms.

title: CRISPR screens reveal MCT1-driven metabolic escape from SMAD3 inhibition as a therapeutic vulnerability.
authors: Matvere, Antti; Menchon, Gregory; Martinetti, Laetitia; Menant, Amelie; Callac, Loan; Ferrari, Hugo; Jarry, Ulrich; Gourdel, Mathilde; Bore, Aurelien; Chassignolle, Morgane; Le Bars, Victor; Cadieu, Edouard; Derrien, Thomas; Aubry, Marc; Gilot, David; Pedeux, Remy
abstract: Resistance to therapy remains a critical challenge in cancer. This is exemplified by TGF-beta pathway inhibitors which, despite broad clinical testing, have failed to deliver survival benefit. More precise SMAD3 targeting has shown preclinical promise, yet resistance mechanisms to SMAD3 inhibition remain entirely unknown. Using complementary genome-wide CRISPR activation and knockout screens, we discover that cancer cells escape SMAD3 inhibition through metabolic reprogramming. Strikingly, this escape is driven not by transcriptional bypass but by the lactate transporter MCT1, with the effect preserved across BRAF-mutated melanoma, KRAS-mutated lung adenocarcinoma, and mouse melanoma. Mechanistically, SMAD3 inhibition creates energetic stress that cancer cells exploit through MCT1. By conferring metabolic flexibility and switching toward glycolysis under drug pressure, MCT1 increases anabolic activity to drive lipid and cholesterol synthesis. Pharmacological and genetic MCT1 inhibition synergizes strongly with SMAD3 blockade to impair tumor viability in BRAF-mutated melanoma, while suppressing drug-tolerant cell emergence in BRAF inhibitor-resistant cells. Critically, this synergy extends to preclinical models, where co-inhibition of SMAD3 and MCT1 potently reduces tumor growth in vivo. Given the additional and well-established role of MCT1 in shaping the tumor immune microenvironment via lactate transport, these results position MCT1 as both a metabolic and immunological target and provide a strong rationale for the repurposing of TGF-beta/SMAD3 pathway inhibitors in combination.

title: Post-Transcriptional Silencing of PHD2 by CRISPR-Cas13d Enhances Pro-Angiogenic Signaling in Human Endothelial Cells.
authors: Terra, Sara Carolina Vieira; Bartolomeo, Cynthia Silvia; Sales, Sofia Mila Cantu de; Inez, Daniel Casartelli de Santa; Torres, Davi Coe; Weinlich, Ricardo; Stilhano, Roberta Sessa
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) reduces tissue perfusion and causes ischemia, conditions in which hypoxia-responsive pathways have an important adaptive role. Hypoxia- inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1alpha), a central regulator of this response, is tightly controlled by prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), encoded by EGLN1. Here, we used an RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13d system to downregulate EGLN1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) under normoxia and hypoxia. METHODS: A PHD2-knockdown (PHD2-KD) HUVEC line was generated by lentiviral delivery of an EGLN1-targeting RNA guide, alongside non-transduced (CTRL) and non-targeting gRNA (NTG) control lines. Molecular and functional assays assessed hypoxia-related signaling, metabolic activity, migration, and sprouting responses under normoxia and hypoxia. RESULTS: Western blotting confirmed a marked reduction in PHD2 protein abundance in PHD2-KD cells relative to both CTRL and NTG cells. PHD2-KD HUVECs exhibited increased VEGFA transcript levels (6.5-fold under normoxia and 5.3-fold under hypoxia) and secreted VEGF concentrations (6.6-fold and 9.4-fold, respectively), together with early increases in HIF1A transcript and HIF-1alpha protein levels and lower TNF-alpha concentrations. Functional assays showed higher metabolic activity, faster wound closure (2.0-fold under normoxia and 2.2-fold under hypoxia), and enhanced sprouting, with up to 7.2-fold more sprouts per bead and sprouts up to 2.7-fold longer than those formed by CTRL. DISCUSSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated EGLN1 targeting reduced PHD2 protein abundance and was associated with higher endothelial metabolic activity, faster wound closure, enhanced sprouting behavior, and lower TNF-alpha secretion. CONCLUSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated downregulation of EGLN1/PHD2 was associated with increased pro-angiogenic signaling and improved angiogenesis-related endothelial responses in vitro, supporting RNA-targeting strategies to modulate hypoxia-responsive pathways.

title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs.
authors: Zhou, Liqun; Renauer, Paul A; Tang, Kaiyuan; Li, Shanshan; Luo, Zhicheng; Feng, Yanzhi; Lin, Shawn H; Zhang, Feifei; Park, Daniel; Fang, Shao-Yu; Vest, Grace; Zhao, Zhihan; Dorst, William; Yang, Luojia; Dong, Chuanpeng; Pan, Xingxin; Klemm, Lars; Yi, S Stephen; Sahni, Nidhi; Peng, Lei; Muschen, Markus; Zhou, Xiaoyu; Chen, Sidi
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells(1-4). Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells(5-9). These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1-SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis.
authors: Kresse, Isaac J; Sayegh, Natalie Y; Munsamy-Govender, Vanisha; Na, Allen; Nitz, Samuel; Ozakman, Yaprak; Bosch, Barbara; Gonzalez Behn-Eschenburg, Sebastian; Poulton, Nicholas C; Reddy, Abhijna K; Wallach, Joshua; Aguilera Olvera, Rodrigo; Castro, Anthony; Kim, Heather; Wong, Andrew I; Tornow, S Nicolai; Bueler, Stephanie A; Law, Wayne W H; Glickman, Michael S; Rubinstein, John L; Schnappinger, Dirk; DeJesus, Michael A; Rock, Jeremy M
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world's deadliest pathogen(1). Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations(2,3). Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein-protein interaction predictions(4) for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells.
authors: Mori, Yoshio; Sakata, Masafumi; Nakatsu, Yuichiro; Hori, Takeshi; Ino, Yoko; Suzuki, Satoshi; Nishi, Mayuko; Kawase, Miyuki; Kakizaki, Masatoshi; Nagai, Misato; Fukano, Kento; Aizaki, Hideki; Hayashi, Hironori; Murayama, Kazutaka; Kodama, Eiichi N; Taguwa, Shuhei; Okura, Takashi; Takahashi, Tatsuki; Kamitani, Wataru; Shirato, Kazuya; Isogawa, Masanori; Kimura, Yayoi; Kaji, Hirokazu; Matsuura, Yoshiharu; Ryo, Akihide
abstract: Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome(1). Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors(2), which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR-Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal-fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

title: Optimization and application of a tetracycline-inducible gene expression system in Kluyveromyces marxianus.
authors: Wang, Jingqi; Zhao, Baixiang; Zeng, Junyuan; Zhou, Jungang; Lu, Hong; Yu, Yao
abstract: Kluyveromyces marxianus is a promising microbial cell factory owing to its rapid growth, thermotolerance, broad carbon-source utilization, and food-safe status. Tetracycline (Tet)-inducible systems provide powerful means for precise gene regulation in various hosts. However, Tet systems with strong induction and low leakiness remain poorly developed in K. marxianus. Here, we optimized a Tet-inducible system in K. marxianus by engineering promoter-Tet-operator architectures. The optimized rtTA-based system achieved up to 14-fold induction, exhibited a rapid response within 20 min, and functioned robustly across different temperatures and culture media. This system enabled efficient induction of genomic gene expression and supported higher heterologous protein production compared with constitutive promoters. Furthermore, we developed a TetR-based inducible guide RNA promoter derived from the native K. marxianus tRNA(Gly) promoter, enabling low-leakage CRISPR-based gene disruption, activation, and interference. Together, these tools expand the genetic toolbox for precise gene regulation in both fundamental and industrial applications in K. marxianus. KEY POINTS: A strong, rapid and robust Tet-inducible system was optimized in K. marxianus. The system efficiently induced genomic genes and heterologous protein expression. An inducible guide RNA promoter used for low-leakage CRISPR-based gene regulation.

title: Fast and accurate resolution of ecDNA sequence using Cycle-Extractor.
authors: Faizrahnemoon, Mahsa; Luebeck, Jens; Hung, King L; Rao, Suhas; Prasad, Gino; Wong, Ivy Tsz-Lo; Kandarpa, Hitesh; Jones, Matthew G; Mischel, Paul S; Chang, Howard Y; Zhu, Kaiyuan; Bafna, Vineet
abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) plays a key role in cancer pathology. ecDNAs mediate high oncogene amplification and expression and are associated with worse patient outcomes. Accurately determining the structure of these circular molecules is essential for understanding their function, yet reconstructing ecDNA cycles from sequencing data remains challenging. We introduce Cycle-Extractor (CE) for this task. CE takes as input a breakpoint graph derived from either short or long read sequencing data and extracts cycles of maximum length-weighted copy number. CE utilizes a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) and a separate traversal procedure, enabling fast optimization and compatibility with open-source ILP solvers. We evaluated CE against CoRAL (long-read, mixed-integer quadratically constrained programming), Decoil (long-reads), and AmpliconArchitect (AA; short reads) on both simulated data and real cancer cell lines. On simulated ecDNA, CE achieves accuracy comparable to CoRAL across three metrics and consistently outperforms AA and Decoil. On cancer cell lines, CE produces longer and heavier cycles than AA, and performs comparably to CoRAL, while being on average 40x faster. These results demonstrate that CE accurately reconstructs ecDNA from both short and long-read sequencing data, and that long-read inputs allow CE to recover more complete, higher-confidence ecDNA structures. CE improved the prediction of many ecDNA structures. On PC3 ecDNA containing MYC, CE uses ONT data to reconstruct a substantially larger and higher-copy sequence (4.2 Mbp) compared to the short-read-derived reconstruction (690 kbp). CRISPR-CATCH experiments confirm the presence of a large ecDNA molecule, validating the long-read-based CE reconstruction.

title: Ecological and Molecular Basis of Capripoxvirus Cross-Host Transmission: From Transmission Networks to Adaptive Evolution.
authors: He, Zhiyang; Zhang, Jingjing; Kuang, Siping; Li, Shuli; Chen, Junjie; Yang, Junfeng; Ma, Zhenghai; Ding, Juntao; Zhang, Beibei; Zhang, Yanping
abstract: BACKGROUND: Capripoxvirus (CaPV), comprising sheeppox virus (SPPV), goatpox virus (GTPV) and lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV), represents a growing transboundary threat to global livestock, with expanding geographic distribution and increasingly prominent cross-species transmission in mixed farming systems. OBJECTIVES: This review systematically examines the multifaceted drivers of CaPV spillover from ecological, molecular and evolutionary perspectives. METHODS: This review integrates ecological, molecular and evolutionary analyses, incorporating mathematical modelling and summarising advances in CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics. RESULTS: Ecologically, a tripartite network involving habitat sharing, landscape permeability (e.g., forest farmland edges) and arthropod vectors is proposed; mathematical modelling identifies vector-to-host ratio and vaccination coverage as critical modulators of outbreak severity. Molecularly, genetic plasticity in terminal genomic regions (e.g., ankyrin family) and host range genes (HRGs) such as M062R, M159, and LSDV012 enable antagonism of host restriction factors including SAMD9, IFIT1 and PKR, with the C7L superfamily playing a pivotal role in breaching species barriers. Evolutionarily, recombination-driven diversification, immune selection pressure and genetic bottlenecks collectively shape adaptive radiation and frequent host jumping events. Advances in CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics are summarised. However, live attenuated vaccines show limitations in safety and efficacy. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Persistent challenges include ecological surveillance, molecular discrimination of the three species and vaccine-wild type recombination risks. By integrating these disciplines, this review offers a comprehensive framework for understanding CaPV cross-species transmission and supports the design of precision control strategies targeting ecological and molecular vulnerabilities.

title: The plasmid arsenal within: Type IV-A CRISPR-Cas systems in Enterobacteriaceae as modulators of resistance and virulence.
authors: Ghoreyshizadeh, Erfan; Namaki, Malek; Naeimi, Fariba; Sedaghat, Farzaneh Rafie; Rezaee, Mohammad Ahangarzadeh; Kafil, Hossein Samadi
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases
abstract: The Enterobacteriaceae family, which includes prominent pathogens such as K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and S. enterica, poses a significant global health threat due to the rapid dissemination of multidrug resistance and virulence determinants. Central to this dissemination are conjugative plasmids, which act as vehicles for horizontal gene transfer. Among the myriad defense systems that interact with these mobile genetic elements, the type IV-A CRISPR-Cas system stands out due to its enigmatic nature and unique plasmid-centric biology. Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems that are chromosomal and target bacteriophages, type IV-A systems are predominantly encoded on large, conjugative plasmids, particularly those bearing IncHI1B/IncFIB replicons. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology of type IV-A systems within Enterobacteriaceae, elucidating their role as mediators of inter-plasmid competition, their paradoxical association with the spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, and their emerging applications as programmable tools. We explore the mechanistic basis for their function as a natural CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) system, the epidemiological landscape of their distribution, and the dual role they play in both constraining and facilitating the dissemination of clinically relevant traits. Finally, we propose ambitious research avenues, including the development of "plasmid-destroying" probiotics, the use of type IV-A systems as epidemiological biosensors, and the exploration of hypotheses concerning their role in mediating bacterial "altruism" or serving as a "genetic memory" of the plasmid "secretoome."

title: Bifunctional cytochrome P450/ferredoxin is required for fungal phytochrome assembly at mitochondria.
authors: Schuhmacher, Lars; Landmark, Alexander; Jahring, Tim; Muller, Anna; Streng, Christian; Fischer, Reinhard
abstract: Mitochondria act as dynamic signaling hubs intertwining cellular metabolism and environmental perception in fungi. Here, we elucidate the assembly of the red-light sensing phytochrome (FphA) at the mitochondrial outer membrane in Alternaria alternata. Phytochrome photoconversion strictly relies on biliverdin biosynthesis by heme oxygenases. While mammalian and plant heme oxygenases localize to the endoplasmic reticulum or chloroplasts, the fungal system uniquely repurposes the outer mitochondrial membrane. We demonstrate that the fungal heme oxygenases HoxA and HoxB form a heteromeric complex integrated into the membrane via mitochondrial import machinery components Mim1 and Mim2. At the mitochondrial surface, only HoxA binds directly to FphA. Genomic screening identified Bifunctional Cytochrome P450 Reductase/Ferredoxin A (BcfA) as the essential physiological electron donor. Quantitative kinetics established that BcfA operates as an asymmetric hub, displaying higher affinity for HoxB than HoxA. HoxB functions as a high-affinity kinetic tether locking the donor at the membrane boundary. Consequently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of bcfA disrupts red-light signalling. Thus, a multi-protein mitochondrial complex evolved in fungi to wire light perception through spatial compartmentalization.

title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element.
authors: Shi, Peiguo; Yang, Feiyue; Fnu, Tala; Huang, Wesley; Xing, Linqing; Alam, Shah; Dai, Wangyang; Aparicio, Alexis O; Kalicki, Colin H; Trehan, Aditi; Murphy, Michael R; Rotlevi, Esther R; Iyer, Prajish; Wang, Lili; Zaccara, Sara; Reilly, Muredach P; Liao, Ya Cheng; Zhang, Chaolin; Que, Jianwen; Wu, Xuebing
abstract: Noncoding sequences comprise most of the human genome; however, their functional significance remains largely elusive.
