Using CRISPR tiling mutagenesis with near-PAMless, high-fidelity SpRY-Cas9, we mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene, the 10-kb MYC locus, at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. Essential noncoding base pairs are under strong constraint in the human population but show limited evolutionary conservation across species. Within this landscape, we identified an ultraconserved noncoding RNA element in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) that promotes perinuclear localization of MYC mRNA and nuclear localization of MYC protein through interaction with hnRNP L. Steric-blocking antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting this element selectively eliminate diverse MYC-dependent cancer cells and inhibit growth of patient-derived tumor organoids. Together, these findings establish noncoding sequences as major carriers of functional genetic information and identify a therapeutically actionable RNA element whose targeting disrupts MYC-driven cancer.

title: OsDREB1B regulates cold and salt stress responses in rice (Oryza sativa L.).
authors: Cheng, Yishan; Garcia-Caparros, Pedro; Li, Xiujie; Wu, Youlong; Liu, Binke; Li, Yunyu; Zhao, Minghui; Guo, Zhifu
abstract: Dehydration-responsive element-binding (DREB) transcription factors play central roles in plant adaptation to abiotic stresses; however, the stress-specific functions and regulatory mechanisms of individual DREB members in rice remain incompletely understood. Here, we conducted a systematic analysis of the rice DREB gene family and identified OsDREB1B as a stress-responsive transcription factor involved in cold and salt stress responses. OsDREB1B contains a conserved AP2 DNA-binding domain and is transcriptionally induced by cold, salt, and PEG-induced osmotic stress. Subcellular localization assays revealed that OsDREB1B displays stress-dependent localization, with dual localization in the nucleus and plasma membrane under normal conditions and predominant nuclear accumulation under cold stress. Functional analyses using two independent CRISPR/Cas9-generated loss-of-function alleles demonstrated that disruption of OsDREB1B increased sensitivity to cold and salt stresses, as reflected by reduced survival rate, increased H(2)O(2) and O(2)(*-) accumulation, impaired antioxidant enzyme activities, and increased membrane damage. In contrast, osmotic stress was largely unaffected despite transcriptional induction of OsDREB1B under PEG-induced osmotic stress. Collectively, these results demonstrate that OsDREB1B positively contributes to cold and salt stress responses in rice and reveal a cold-associated change in its subcellular distribution.

title: Generation of CD43-P2A-mNeonGreen reporter human pluripotent stem cell line using CRISPR Cas9.
authors: van der Stel, M; Adriaanssen, V E; Flierman, S; Brosens, E; Philipsen, J N J; van den Akker, E; Varga, E
abstract: This study presents a human induced pluripotent stem cell line engineered to report endogenous CD43 expression by mNeonGreen presence, e.g. enabling visualization of hematopoietic emergence during the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition. To create this resource, Cas9 ribonucleoprotein targeting the SPN locus and a PCR amplified homology-directed-repair template were used to introduce the reporter sequence, followed by clonal isolation and molecular characterization. The resulting line maintains pluripotency, genomic integrity, and trilineage differentiation potential. This resource accurately reports CD43(+) cells during hematopoietic organoid differentiation, supporting applications in studying CD43 + expression dynamics.

title: Complete genome analysis, safety assessment and probiotic potential of Limosilactobacillus oris BSLO1801.
authors: Duan, Lixiao; Zhang, Yiming; Zhou, Mengjia; Wan, Zhiqiang; Zhou, Yanxi; Pan, Kangcheng; Zeng, Dong; Jing, Bo; Shu, Gang; Zeng, Yan; Ni, Xueqin
abstract: Clarifying the genomic information of probiotic strains is an important prerequisite for their application. Limosilactobacillus oris BSLO1801 (BSLO1801), a strain derived from the manure of high-yield laying hens, has shown promise in enhancing the performance of poultry and is considered for use as a feed additive. This research assessed the safety profile and probiotic attributes of BSLO1801 through a combination of in vitro and in vivo experiments, complemented by whole-genome sequencing analysis. The genomic evaluation revealed that BSLO1801 comprises a single chromosome and five plasmids, and it lacks CRISPR sequences, classical virulence factors, and oriT transfer sites. Among the 17 antibiotic resistance genes identified, only plasmid-borne tet (M) was classified as an acquired resistance gene, while the other 16 were intrinsic chromosomal resistance genes. The genome was thoroughly annotated with databases such as COG, GO, KEGG, CAZy, identifying a wealth of genes associated with probiotic functionalities, particularly those involved in carbohydrate metabolism. In vitro assays showed BSLO1801 had good gastrointestinal tolerance and moderate EPS/DPPH antioxidant activity; its adhesion measured on human Caco-2 cells cannot directly represent avian intestinal performance, and no haemolysis was observed., while exhibiting no haemolytic properties. No significant changes in body weight or organ indices were observed in mice following oral administration of BSLO1801. In conclusion, no adverse effects were observed for BSLO1801 under all tested conditions; this strain possesses favorable in vitro probiotic properties and comprehensively annotated genomic features, making it a promising candidate for subsequent validation as a poultry feed-additive probiotic.

title: Erratum for the Research Article "CRISPR-engineered human brown-like adipocytes prevent diet-induced obesity and ameliorate metabolic syndrome in mice".
Genetic dissection of cell type-specific congenital heart disease variants reveals ETS1 control of vascular smooth muscle cell fate.
authors: Li, Xin; Fu, Mingzhu; Jia, Shengtao; Wu, Zhenwei; Pang, Long; Xiong, Ke; Wang, Yujun; Li, Wen; He, Aibin; Ai, Shanshan
abstract: Numerous congenital heart disease (CHD) risk variants lie in cis-regulatory elements, yet the impact of variants in repressed and bivalent chromatin on cell type-specific heart development is unclear. Here, we generated a single-cell multiomic atlas of human cardiac differentiation by jointly profiling H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and transcriptomes in individual cells, classifying cis-regulatory elements into six chromatin states, enabling prioritization of 610 CHD-associated noncoding variants enriched in lineage- and state-specific regulatory elements, including repressive and bivalent regions. CRISPR knockin of selected variants perturbed nearby gene expression and impaired cardiac differentiation. Dissection of a Polycomb-marked variant near ETS1 (ETS proto-oncogene 1) revealed local H3K27me3 loss, H3K27ac gain, and ETS1 up-regulation, which redirects differentiation toward second-heart-field progenitors with epithelial characteristics at early stages and, ultimately, highly migratory ETS1(+) vascular smooth muscle cells. Together, our work establishes a single-cell chromatin-state framework for interpreting noncoding CHD risk variants and uncovers an ETS1-driven program linking Polycomb-deregulated noncoding variation to aberrant vascular smooth muscle fate commitment during human cardiogenesis.

title: Integrated Single-Step Duplex CRISPR-Based System for Point-of-Care Detection of Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Treponema pallidum Directly from Whole Blood.
authors: Xu, Ziwen; Wang, Yunxiang; Wei, Muyun; Miao, Ping; Zhang, Haomin; Li, Min; Wang, Shengqi; Rong, Zhen; He, Kunlun
abstract: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and syphilis are two major sexually transmitted diseases that pose serious threats to public health, underscoring the urgent need for fast and sensitive diagnosis for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and Treponema pallidum (TP). Here, we developed a single-step duplex CRISPR assay that integrated reverse transcription, recombinase polymerase amplification, in vitro transcription, and CRISPR/Cas12a and Cas13a detection for simultaneous HIV and TP nucleic acid testing. We further engineered a fully integrated, low-cost microfluidic chip that consolidated whole-blood sample processing, nucleic acid release, and single-step duplex CRISPR detection. The chip featured a rapid plasma separator with a press-actuated design that removed inhibitors and extracted plasma within minutes without external equipment. The entire process was coupled with a homemade smartphone-based portable device that provided thermal incubation, dual-channel fluorescence excitation, and automated image analysis via a dedicated mobile application. This integrated system enables "sample-to-answer" detection within 30 min directly from whole blood, achieving a limit of detection of 2.5 copies/muL of both HIV and TP and demonstrating 100% sensitivity and specificity concordant with the real-time PCR in 51 cases of clinical samples. This work demonstrates a transformative point-of-care diagnostic platform that combines minimal user steps, equipment independence, and robust multiplex detection for decentralized pathogen testing.

title: Programmed bacterial lysis in vivo alters host immune responses and microbial pathogenesis.
authors: Lembke, Mareike; Simmons, Daimon P; Robins, William P; Toska, Jonida; Meader, Bradley T; Mekalanos, John J
abstract: Vibrio cholerae injects toxic type VI secretion system (T6SS) effectors to lyse sensitive intestinal commensals, but how this bacterial antagonism enhances mucosal host immune responses and its pathogenicity remains unknown. To mimic T6SS-mediated killing, we engineered V. cholerae lysis strains by using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to knockdown essential genes in peptidoglycan biogenesis or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport. Our results indicate that controlled bacterial lysis in vivo leads to divergent mucosal immune responses that directly modulate colonization and pathogenicity of a bystander, non-lysing V. cholerae DeltaT6SS strain. Mass spectrometric analysis of the lysis debris revealed proinflammatory muropeptides correlating with these changes. We confirmed that oral co-administration of a synthetic peptidoglycan-derived metabolite with a V. cholerae DeltaT6SS mutant, but not the wild type, shows dramatic enhancement of disease symptoms. These findings show that intestinal exposure to discrete bacterial cell wall metabolites can differentially modulate host innate immune responses and consequently bacterial pathogenesis.

title: Breeding the unbreedable: bottlenecks and genetic pathways to climate-resilient saffron (Crocus sativus L.).
authors: Sofi, Mehrajuddin; Reshi, Saika Mushtaq; Khan, Mudasir Hafiz; Qureshi, Asif Mohd Iqbal; Mustafa, Soliha; Butter, Baljinder Singh
abstract: Cultivated saffron (Crocus sativus L.) is a sterile autotriploid clone (2n = 3x = 24), propagated by corm division for roughly 3,600 years from a single auto-triploidisation event. Sequence-level polymorphism across the global crop is barely 4%, and no F2, recombinant inbred, QTL, or GWAS population has ever been produced, because triploid meiosis forecloses recombination-based breeding outright. This genetic standstill coincides with an accelerating production crisis: Kashmir has lost over 70% of its historical stigma yield, and global stigma yield has fallen by roughly 35% over recent decades. Methylation polymorphism across the World Saffron and Crocus Collection is eight-fold higher than sequence polymorphism, making epigenetic divergence the only substantial non-mutagenic source of heritable variation currently accessible. Heat, drought, cold, and Fusarium-driven disease converge on the florigen activation complex and the apocarotenoid pathway, defining a compact target set led by CsatSVP2, CsCCD2, and a defined NBS-LRR resistance-gene catalogue. Against the genomic infrastructure now available, including a fully phased 8.42 Gb triploid assembly, we evaluate the strategies open to this crop: epigenomic selection, clean-stock reform, induced mutagenesis, soma-clonal selection, wild-relative pre-breeding, and CRISPR/base/prime editing. Improvement is no longer limited mainly by a shortage of molecular targets or tools, but by a small number of translational bottlenecks, foremost the absence of any published whole-plant regeneration pipeline for edited tissue. We rank these bottlenecks by dependency and set out our own view of research priorities for the next five to fifteen years.

title: OsGAT2 modulates nitrogen allocation and heading date in rice through amino acid transport.
authors: Yang, Xiaochuan; He, Chongchong; Ming, Zhaoyong; Wu, Bowen; Luo, Hangfei; Huang, Weiting; Fang, Zhongming
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
abstract: Heading date (or flowering time) is one of the most important agronomic traits in rice, as it determines regional adaptability and grain yield. Its regulation is influenced by multiple factors, including photoperiod, nutritional status, and endogenous phytohormones. However, the roles of amino acids and their transporters in regulating heading date remain largely unclear. In this study, we identified four haplotypes in the promoter region of the rice amino acid transporter gene OsGAT2 among diverse germplasm resources. Haplotypes associated with lower OsGAT2 expression exhibited earlier heading date, longer grain length, and reduced nitrogen content. Further analyses showed that OsGAT2 is mainly expressed in basal tissues, stems, and leaf sheaths, and is localized to the plasma membrane. Substrate assays in yeast demonstrated that OsGAT2 is capable of transporting multiple amino acids, including GABA, Ser, Leu, Glu, Val, Gly, and Ala. Functional analyses revealed that knockout of OsGAT2 promoted earlier heading date, whereas overexpression lines exhibited delayed heading date. Consistently, the contents of GABA, several amino acids, and total nitrogen in the leaves and panicles were significantly higher in OsGAT2 overexpression lines than in the wild-type, whereas OsGAT2 CRISPR knockout lines exhibited tissue-dependent changes, with increased stem nitrogen content but reduced nitrogen content in leaves and panicles. Moreover, exogenous application of these amino acids further enhanced the delayed heading date phenotype in overexpression lines, while mutants headed earlier than the wild-type. Transcriptome analysis revealed that altered expression of OsGAT2 affects the regulatory network controlling heading date. The heading repressors Ghd7 and Ghd8 were significantly upregulated in OsGAT2 overexpression lines but downregulated in mutants. In contrast, heading-promoting genes, including OsGI, Hd17, and Ehd2, were markedly upregulated in the mutants. Taken together, these results demonstrate that the amino acid transporter OsGAT2 regulates rice heading date by mediating amino acid transport and modulating the expression of key heading regulatory genes. This study provides important insights and potential targets for shortening heading time and improving regional adaptability of rice through gene editing. KEY MESSAGE : The amino acid transporter gene OsGAT2 regulates rice heading date by modulating amino acid transport and the expression of heading date-related genes, thereby improving regional adaptability.

title: Dual-mode biosensing featuring fluorescence and electrochemiluminescence for regional resolution of single-nucleotide variants.
authors: Yang, Huan; Lai, Tingting; Zhang, Hui; Zhan, Minhan; Chen, Shuhan; Zhang, Ximei; Chen, Lanlan; Hu, Shanwen
abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) are a critical molecular basis for antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria. However, precise detection of mutant targets remains challenging because they may exist at low abundance and often coexist with wild-type sequences in complex biological matrices. Herein, we report a target-triggered strand displacement reaction that releases two functional DNA strands: one activates the trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR/Cas12a to generate a fluorescent signal, while the other competitively displaces cadmium sulfide quantum dots pre-modified on a gold electrode surface, decreasing the electrochemiluminescence (ECL) signal. The two functional strands hybridize to distinct regions of the probe, enabling the two signaling channels to respond differentially to single-base mismatches at different locations. Taking the response to wild-type targets as a reference, synchronized changes in both signals reflect target concentration. A significant decrease in the fluorescence signal alone, with the ECL signal unchanged, indicates that the mismatch occurs within the fluorescence recognition region, whereupon the unaffected ECL channel may serve for quantification. Conversely, when the ECL signal decreases while the fluorescence signal remains stable, the fluorescence channel may serve for quantification. This design enables a single probe to discriminate between wild-type and mutant targets based on the differential responses of the two signaling channels. Our strategy thus provides a new avenue for single-base nucleic acid detection.

title: Magnetic bead-assisted DSN/CRISPR-Cas12a fluorescence biosensor for sensitive and specific detection of miRNA-122.
authors: Yu, Zhen; Wang, Jin; An, Yacong; Wu, Jing; Du, Shuangshuang; Wu, Yujing; Wang, Jiajian; Zhang, Jiandong
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: MicroRNA-122 (miR-122) is a liver-enriched miRNA closely associated with hepatic disorders, making its sensitive detection crucial for liver disease-related biomarker analysis. Herein, we report a magnetic bead-assisted duplex-specific nuclease (DSN) cleavage strategy coupled with CRISPR/Cas12a fluorescence biosensing for sensitive miR-122 detection. A biotinylated DNA probe containing both a miR-122 recognition region and a Cas12a activator region was immobilized on streptavidin-modified magnetic beads. Upon target hybridization, DSN selectively cleaved the RNA/DNA duplex, releasing the DNA activator while enabling miR-122 recycling. After magnetic separation, the released activator triggered Cas12a-mediated trans-cleavage of a fluorophore-quencher-labeled ssDNA reporter, generating a fluorescence turn-on signal. Under optimized conditions, the biosensor showed a linear response from 100 fM to 10 nM, with a detection limit of 85 fM. The assay exhibited high specificity against mismatched sequences and other miRNAs, and achieved satisfactory recoveries (93.0-95.3%, RSD < 8%) in 10% human serum. This magnetic bead-assisted DSN/CRISPR-Cas12a fluorescence biosensor provides a simple, sensitive, and specific platform for miR-122 detection, holding promise for liver disease-related diagnostic applications.

title: FASTOP horizontal line Fast Editing Toolkit for Top Expression Sites in Yeast.
authors: Borah, Madhushruti; Gautron, Nicolas; Courdavault, Vincent; Naseri, Gita
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a widely used chassis for producing food- and agriculture-related compounds, but construction of multienzyme pathways often requires repeated genomic integration. We developed FASTOP, a genome-editing toolkit for rapid engineering of eight transcriptionally active genomic hot-spot loci. FASTOP combines selectable markers, extended homology arms, and Cas9/gRNA-assisted integration, and enables PCR-free release of donor cassettes by restriction digestion to reduce sequence errors introduced during amplification. After characterizing the sites, we integrated a five-gene naringenin biosynthetic pathway into the hot spots as a proof of concept. Our results demonstrated that, upon expressing the five essential genes in simple shake-flask culture, naringenin production reached 505.7 mg/L, 6-fold higher than an episomal control expressing the same pathway genes and 4.5-fold higher than the previously reported strain using additional precursor engineering and controlled bioreactor cultivation. FASTOP therefore provides a practical platform for the rapid assembly of multienzyme pathways in yeast for stable heterologous gene expression.

title: Anthocyanin Biosynthesis, Multilayered Regulation, and Biotechnological Applications in Fruits.
authors: Zhu, Jiani; Wu, Ying; Chen, Xuyang; Li, Xiang; Zhang, Guiyu; Xu, Shuxin; Lin, Yiru; Wu, Xuying; Li, Yuanyuan; Zheng, Bingsong; Ni, Junbei; Shi, Kai; Cui, Fuqiang; Wang, Jiao
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Anthocyanins are water-soluble flavonoid pigments that confer vivid coloration to fruits and provide multiple health benefits. Here, we critically review recent advances in the structural diversity, biosynthetic pathways, and multilayered regulation of fruit anthocyanins. We summarize the enzymatic and postsynthetic modifications that determine pigment stability, and examine the MYB-bHLH-WD40 (MBW) complex, its interplay with NAC, WRKY, ERF, and bZIP factors, and the roles of epigenetic and post-translational controls. Hormonal, environmental, and nutrient signals are integrated into a unified model, emphasizing the contrasting regulatory logics of climacteric versus nonclimacteric fruits and the tissue specificity of peel- vs flesh-localized pigmentation. We evaluate biotechnological strategies, including CRISPR-based precision breeding, microbial cell factories, and plant metabolic engineering, highlighting both transformative potential and translational bottlenecks. Finally, we propose future directions for translating fundamental knowledge into anthocyanin-enriched fruits and sustainable production systems for the food and health industries.

title: SlABCB13 Regulates Hexose and Sucrose Homeostasis during Tomato Fruit Development.
authors: Xie, Xiao; Xie, Na; Qi, Tian; Liu, Pengfei; Li, Qiuhui; Qiao, Hongyu; Wang, Wei; Zhang, Xinsheng
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Sugar accumulation in fleshy fruits is largely dependent on membrane-localized sugar transporters, among which SWEET proteins play important roles. Although ABCB transporters, a subclass of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily, mediate the transport of diverse substrates and participate in various physiological processes in plants, their direct involvement in fruit sugar accumulation remains unclear. In this study, SlABCB13, an ABCB transporter in tomato, was characterized. Multiple in vitro and in vivo assays demonstrated that SlABCB13 physically interacts with SlSWEET14. SlABCB13 was predominantly expressed in fruits and localized to the plasma membrane. Heterologous expression in yeast showed that SlABCB13 transported fructose and glucose, but not sucrose. Genetic analysis revealed that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of SlABCB13 significantly increased fruit hexose, sucrose, and total sugar contents while reducing fruit weight. SlABCB13-overexpressing lines also demonstrated reduced fruit weight, accompanied by stage-specific alterations in sugar levels. Transcriptome analysis revealed distinct transcriptional reprogramming in SlABCB13 knockout and overexpression lines, characterized by downregulation of sugar transporter genes in the overexpression lines, consistent with feedback inhibition, and upregulation in the knockout lines, indicative of compensatory activation. These results identify SlABCB13 as a plant ABCB transporter that mediates hexose transport in yeast and as an important regulator of sugar homeostasis in tomato fruits through coordinated feedback and compensatory mechanisms. This study broadens the functional spectrum of ABCB transporters and highlights SlABCB13 as a potential target for molecular breeding to improve fruit quality.

title: Scaffold-level validation is needed for phage-host inference from metagenome-assembled genomes.
authors: Yuan, Ling; Anantharaman, Karthik; Ma, Bin; Camargo, Antonio Pedro; Chen, LinXing
abstract: Accurate phage-host prediction underpins ecological interpretation and experimental validation of uncultivated phages, yet most current approaches rely heavily on metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). This reliance implicitly assumes that MAG-level quality metrics, such as completeness and contamination, ensure scaffold-level correctness. Here, we demonstrate that this assumption can be violated under particular challenging conditions. Tetranucleotide frequency (TNF) analyses reveal that CRISPR-associated regions often diverge compositionally from their host genomes, increasing the risk of misbinning, while experimentally validated phage-host genome pairs show consistent TNF separation between phages and their hosts, challenging compositional binning assumptions. Through controlled simulations, we further show that the incorporation of substantial amounts of TNF-matched, non-host phage sequences into high-quality MAGs does not substantially alter standard completeness and contamination estimates, rendering such errors largely undetectable. Together, these results expose a systematic and underappreciated source of bias in MAG-based phage-host inference and highlight the need for explicit scaffold-level validation beyond conventional genome-quality metrics. We further propose a practical scaffold-level validation framework that integrates structural linkage and taxonomic consistency to improve the reliability of phage-host inference from MAGs.

title: Expanding arsenal of type III CRISPR-Cas antiviral defense.
authors: Mogila, Irmantas; Smalakyte, Dalia; Tamulaitis, Gintautas
abstract: CRISPR-Cas systems are adaptive immune systems that protect prokaryotes from invading genetic elements through acquisition of foreign nucleic acid sequences and RNA-guided recognition of target molecules. Among the diverse CRISPR-Cas families, type III systems represent a highly complex and versatile branch that couples sequence-specific interference with nucleotide-based signaling and activation of diverse downstream immune responses. Recent discoveries have substantially expanded the functional diversity of type III CRISPR-Cas systems, revealing new subtypes, ancillary effectors, nucleotide second messengers, signal-degrading enzymes, and viral counter-defense strategies. Here, we summarize current mechanistic and structural insights into type III CRISPR-Cas biology, from adaptation and target recognition to immune signaling, ancillary effector-mediated responses, and defense regulation. We further discuss emerging biotechnological applications of type III systems and highlight key unanswered questions shaping future research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Recombinant Fusion of Polyglutamic Acid Enhances Cell-Penetrating Peptide-Mediated CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery.
authors: Sharma, Amitesh; Seo, Yeeun; Park, Tae-Sik
abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

title: [Specific treatment of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy: established disease-modifying agents and emerging mechanisms].
authors: Najaf Zadeh, Shabnam; Hundertmark, Moritz
abstract: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), in which fibrillary protein deposits accumulate in the cardiac extracellular space, has changed within a few years from a rare condition regarded as therapeutically futile into a causally treatable and increasingly recognised cause of heart failure. Every specific therapy requires a secure diagnosis, with prior exclusion of alternative causes such as light-chain (AL) amyloidosis. Two mechanistic principles are central to the approved treatment options: stabilisation of the transthyretin (TTR) tetramer (Vyndaqel(R), Beyonttra(R)) and reduction of hepatic production through TTR gene silencing (Amvuttra(R)). For the stabilisers and the siRNA agent vutrisiran, randomised trials demonstrate a reduction in all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events; the survival benefit typically becomes apparent months after commencing treatment thus, arguing for the earliest possible initiation of treatment. Two further promising approaches are currently under investigation in phase III trials: antibody-mediated depletion of already deposited amyloid (so-called <<depleters>>) and one-time gene editing (using CRISPR-Cas9). Both offer, for the first time, the prospect of a meaningful regression of amyloid burden and thus of a degree of regression in disease stage. This article classifies the approved agents by mechanism in a practice-oriented manner, discusses the selection, sequencing and combination of therapies as well as the monitoring of treatment response, and provides an outlook on agents in development.

title: The potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) transcription factor StPHR1 responds to low phosphate stress and regulates phosphorus accumulation.
authors: Zhang, Feng; Gou, Huaijuan; An, Yanlin; Wang, Wenlun; Zhang, Haiyan
abstract: Phosphorus is an essential macronutrient for plant growth and development. Potato is highly sensitive to inorganic phosphate (Pi) availability, yet the function and regulation of StPHR1, a putative core component of plant Pi signaling, remain poorly defined in this crop. Evolutionary analysis, subcellular localization assays, promoter activity analysis, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing, overexpression, and data-independent acquisition proteomics were used to characterize StPHR1. StPHR1 encoded a nuclear-localized MYB-CC transcription factor, whose promoter exhibits preferential activity in root tips and vascular tissues. Loss of StPHR1 function compromised low-Pi tolerance, reduced Pi accumulation in roots and leaves, and inhibited plant growth, whereas StPHR1 overexpression enhanced low-Pi tolerance and increased both tuber number and average tuber weight under conventional fertilized cultivation. Proteomic profiling showed that StPHR1-dependent Pi starvation responses involve metabolic reprogramming, membrane-lipid remodeling, redox homeostasis, and detoxification. These results identify StPHR1 as a key regulator of Pi accumulation and allocation in potato and provide candidate targets and a molecular framework for improving low-Pi adaptation.

title: Editorial: CRISPR/CAS innovations: advancing precision and specificity in plant genetic engineering.
authors: Dionisio, Giuseppe; Tiwari, Siddharth; Jogam, Phanikanth

title: Concurrent loss of RB1 facilitates EGFR-TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant lung cancer by modulating histone crotonylation.
authors: Chen, Sihong; Wang, Xiaoyuan; Xuan, Qihao; Liu, Chang; Su, Youwei; Liu, Zongang; Jia, Lina; Ren, Yi; Cui, Wei; Fan, Xinyu; Wang, Lihui
abstract: Lung cancer harboring epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations exhibits marked heterogeneity in clinical responses to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs), indicating that co-occurring genetic alterations critically influence therapeutic outcomes. However, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we modeled frequent EGFR co-alterations using CRISPR-mediated gene knockout and Tet-On-based gene overexpression in two EGFR-mutant cell lines. Functional screening across cell lines and patient-derived organoids revealed that concurrent loss of retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) significantly reduced sensitivity to EGFR-TKIs. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses further demonstrated that RB1 deficiency induced extensive metabolic reprogramming, leading to decreased intracellular crotonyl-CoA levels and reduced histone crotonylation. Among multiple crotonylation sites, histone H3 lysine 23 crotonylation (H3K23cr) emerged as a critical determinant of EGFR-TKI responsiveness. Mechanistically, decreased H3K23cr was associated with transcriptional repression of PEBP1 and reduced expression of the PEBP1-encoded Raf kinase inhibitor protein (RKIP), thereby sustaining RAF/MEK/ERK pathway activation and attenuating EGFR-TKI efficacy. Importantly, pharmacological restoration of histone crotonylation or inhibition of MAPK signaling effectively resensitized EGFR/RB1 co-mutant models to EGFR-TKIs. Taken together, our findings identify a metabolic-epigenetic mechanism linking RB1 loss to reduced histone crotonylation and EGFR-TKI resistance, highlighting therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities in EGFR/RB1 co-mutant lung cancer.

title: Point-of-care testing in the diagnosis of infectious diseases.
authors: Fang, Quan; Lin, Yuyan; Hu, Guiqi; Hu, Jiangjie; Cheng, Jun; Dai, Yuzhu; Yan, Li; Wu, Xiaohong
abstract: Point-of-care testing (POCT) has emerged as an indispensable diagnostic strategy for addressing the increasing global burden of infectious diseases and the worsening threat of antimicrobial resistance. Owing to prominent advantages such as rapid detection of infectious agents, portability, and ease of accessibility, POCT can effectively address the inherent limitations of traditional laboratory diagnostic workflows. This review summarizes the core technical platforms that underlie current POCT technologies, including lateral flow assays, chemiluminescence immunoassays, isothermal amplification systems, CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostic systems, and microfluidic chip technologies. Furthermore, we describe the key clinical scenarios in which POCT can be applied, including respiratory tract, bloodstream, gastrointestinal, urinary tract, and sexually transmitted infections. We also comprehensively discuss the technical characteristics and clinical applicability of mainstream POCT modalities, including immunochromatography and molecular diagnostics. Despite limitations associated with detection sensitivity, quality control, cost efficiency, and clinical integration, POCT technology continues to undergo consistent improvements. Advances in nanomaterials, microfluidic engineering, and artificial intelligence and continuous improvements in industry standardization have led to increased performance, systematic integration, and intelligent detection in POCT. Given these technological advancements and optimizations, POCT shows promising applicability and is therefore expected to become a core diagnostic tool for both precision clinical management and epidemic prevention and control in public health.

title: Epigenetic and RNA-mediated regulation of plant VOC biosynthesis and signalling.
authors: Boba, Aleksandra; Domanska, Anna; Kulma, Anna; Nowosad, Kamila; Bujak, Henryk; Kostyn, Kamil
abstract: Plants use volatile organic compounds (VOCs) as airborne signals in development, defence, and ecological interactions. Epigenetic mechanisms can influence VOC biosynthesis and, in some experimental systems, plant responses to volatile cues. This review examines chromatin-level mechanisms, particularly DNA methylation and histone modifications, in VOC biosynthesis and responses to volatile cues, together with distinct RNA-level regulation by non-coding RNAs and m(6)A-dependent epitranscriptomic mechanisms. VOC perception can activate rapid signalling events, including Ca(2+) influx and reactive oxygen species production; however, direct mechanistic links between these early responses and subsequent chromatin changes remain unresolved. Changes in promoter DNA methylation and histone acetylation are associated with, and in some systems functionally contribute to, regulation of VOC biosynthesis or defence responses, whereas ncRNA- and m(6)A-dependent mechanisms provide distinct RNA-level regulatory layers. Across diverse plant systems, chromatin states can influence VOC biosynthesis and emission, whereas in a smaller set of exposure studies, volatile cues are accompanied by changes in DNA methylation or histone modifications. Persistent or primed responses have been reported in several systems, but persistence of a phenotype or chromatin mark alone does not establish stress memory, and causal epigenetic involvement in VOC-induced memory remains unresolved. Important knowledge gaps concern the mechanisms linking volatile perception with chromatin regulation, the integration of complex VOC blends, and the relevance of these processes under field conditions. Emerging approaches, including locus-specific CRISPR/dCas-based epigenome editing and temporally resolved multi-omics, should help distinguish causal chromatin mechanisms from downstream transcriptional responses. Current evidence therefore supports distinct chromatin- and RNA-level contributions to VOC biology but does not yet establish a general mechanistic pathway from volatile perception to epigenetically encoded stress memory.

title: Intranasal nano-immunotherapy for glioma: bypassing the blood-brain barrier, reprogramming the immune microenvironment, and bridging preclinical validation.
authors: Li, Leina; Wu, Moli; Li, Liya
abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

title: Genome editing for nutritional biofortification in maize: bridging molecular innovation and food security in the Global South.
authors: Syombua, Easter D; Venado, Rafael E; Achary, V Mohan Murali; Kaur, Simranjit; Palacios Rojas, Natalia; Ibba, Maria Itria; Lewis, Laurajean; Hearne, Sarah J; Bandyopadhyay, Anindya
abstract: Micronutrient deficiency is a prevalent challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa and other geographies of the Global South where populations rely on maize as the primary calorie source. Globally, the most widespread micronutrient deficiencies include iron, zinc, and vitamin A, which are inherently low in maize. Besides, maize grain protein percentage of the essential amino acids falls below the recommended daily allowance. Traditional plant breeding practices have enabled the generation of hybrid plant varieties with superior nutritional value, such as Quality Protein Maize (QPM). However, obtaining novel varieties from existing gene pools often results in linkage drag drawbacks, yield penalties, poor-quality kernels, and requires multiple backcrossing cycles. Thus, genome editing offers a precise strategy for enhancing nutritional value, without the associated trade-offs. CRISPR/Cas, base editors and prime editors reduce breeding timelines and enable precise targeting of nutrient-accumulation pathways. In this review, we explore how genome editing technology could serve as the next-generation approach for maize biofortification. The review outlines various ways CRISPR/Cas allow precise and targeted modification of genes responsible for micronutrient biosynthesis, transport, and storage. We describe the application of CRISPR in disrupting negative regulators of nutrient transport, up-regulating nutrient biosynthesis pathways, and knocking out anti-nutritional factor genes. We further highlight that CRISPR-enabled biofortification is not just a technological innovation but a public health intervention for mitigating nutrient deficiencies. However, fully unlocking the potential of gene-edited biofortified maize will require coordinated efforts in regulatory policy and alignment with farmer/consumer preference.

title: Rational design of lipid nanoparticles for brain delivery of RNA therapeutics.
authors: Tian, Meng; Wang, Leiming; Liu, Zhengwei; Cao, Dinglingge; Yu, Changyue; Bennett, Jeffrey L; Bliss-Moreau, Eliza; Wang, Chang; Kang, Diana D; Xue, Yonger; Zhong, Yichen; Wang, Siyu; Li, Haoyuan; Hou, Xucheng; Deng, Binbin; Dong, Yizhou
abstract: Effective delivery of RNA therapeutics to the brain remains challenging due to the multiple barriers of the central nervous system (CNS). To probe molecular scaffolds that could help overcome these barriers, we analysed the pharmaceutical profiles of over 100 CNS-active drugs and identified hydroxyzine (HX) as a promising scaffold for designing ionizable lipids with improved brain-targeting properties. Specifically, HX1 liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) achieved robust mRNA delivery to the brain through multiple trafficking pathways across CNS barriers. HX1 LNPs also enabled efficient gene editing in mouse brains via co-delivery of CRISPR mRNA and guide RNA and effectively delivered luciferase mRNA to the brain of a non-human primate. Moreover, HX1 LNPs carrying Il10 mRNA mitigated radiation-induced brain injury in mice, highlighting their potential for preventive treatment in the presence of intact CNS barriers. These findings establish HX1 LNPs as a promising translational platform for delivering therapeutic mRNAs and genome-editing components to the brain.

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for beta-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials.
authors: Al-Subaie, Abeer M; Borgio, J Francis
abstract: BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (beta-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics. METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in beta-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes. RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of beta-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance. CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for beta-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global beta-thal and SCD patient care.

title: Combinatorial Tuning of Multigene Biosynthetic Pathways based on RNA Interference.
authors: Zhang, Zixu; Xu, Yingshuang; Li, Zijia; Du, Fei; Ma, Wang; Yang, Guang; Sun, Xiaoman
abstract: Fine-tuning the expression level of multigene pathways remains a major challenge in engineering eukaryotic microbial cell factories. Modifications to individual pathway genes and CRISPR-based approaches often require repeated genome reconstruction, large regulatory components, or complex guide-array assembly. Here, we developed a lightweight, post-transcriptional RNAi-based strategy that enables fine-tuning gene expression without iterative genome editing. Size-selected small-RNA sequencing and functional testing were used to identify endogenous Pol III promoters spanning graded transcriptional strengths in Schizochytrium sp. Combining promoter strength with multiple short hairpin RNA (shRNA) target positions expanded the accessible repression range and enabled high-resolution gene-dosage tuning. The RNAi-based combined regulation strategy was applied to the three-gene carotenoid pathway of Schizochytrium sp. and the nine-gene docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) pathway of Yarrowia lipolytica, significantly enhancing the product production in both hosts. Integration of RNAi screening and dosage optimization further identified and tuned bypass pathways, increasing the ratio of DHA to docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) by 4.50-fold versus wild type. These gains were maintained during 5-L fermentation and serial passaging. This work establishes a compact and scalable regulatory framework for engineering complex biosynthetic pathways in eukaryotic microbial hosts.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.
authors: Stigliano, Jose N; Haberfeld, Emilia; Marasco, Luciano E; Fiszbein, Ana; Proudfoot, Nick J; Kornblihtt, Alberto R
abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: Hyperdivergent haplotypes control melanic camouflage in a polymorphic moth.
authors: Livraghi, Luca; Cassily, Jordan L; Brayer, Mallory; Carter, Alexander T; Alqassar, Jasmine D; Sim, Sheina B; Geib, Scott M; Hanly, Joseph J; Martin, Arnaud
abstract: A majority of moths use melanic pigmentation to blend into the visual environment, and some species display genetically controlled color polymorphisms that provide tractable systems for dissecting the genetic basis of camouflage. Here, we leveraged the natural polymorphism of Anticarsia gemmatalis moths to map a major-effect gene that controls melanic variation and study its developmental roles using expression and loss-of-function assays. Genome-wide association mapping identifies the ivory:mir-193 non-coding RNA locus as a major locus of melanic variation, with highly divergent haplotypes differentiating the Light and Dark morphs. Second, the expression of ivory:mir-193 prefigures the melanic coloration of each morph and suggests that cis-regulatory variation at this locus determines the difference in adult pattern. Finally, CRISPR disruption of the ivory promoter and mir-193 hairpin region each abolishes melanic scale pigmentation, demonstrating that this lnc-pri-miRNA module is required for dark-scale differentiation. These findings corroborate the emerging role of ivory:mir-193 as a key factor in the development of melanic patterning and highlight its unique propensity to repeatedly drive phenotypic variation of adaptive potential in butterflies and moths.

title: Nucleic acid amplification testing for obligate intracellular and cell wall-deficient bacteria: from assay performance to clinical interpretation, a structured narrative review.
authors: Naderi, Mahmood; Sadidi, Roya; Besharati, Reza; Kebriae, Abdollah; Azimian, Amir
abstract: Obligate intracellular bacteria (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Coxiella, Chlamydia) and cell wall-deficient Mycoplasma species present profound diagnostic challenges due to their fastidious growth, low circulating burden, and genomic instability. Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs) have revolutionized detection, yet critical gaps persist in distinguishing active infection from persistent DNA, standardizing cycle threshold interpretation, and integrating host-response biomarkers. This structured narrative review provides a comprehensive analysis of the complete diagnostic armamentarium for these pathogens. It is based on a reproducible, non-systematic literature survey and is not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review. We cover conventional methods (culture, serology), NAAT platforms (qPCR, digital PCR, isothermal amplification), and emerging technologies including CRISPR-Cas diagnostics, metagenomic sequencing, nanopore sequencing, biosensors, and host-response biomarker profiling. We introduce four conceptual frameworks: the "biological noise" paradigm reframing low-copy detection as a signal-to-noise challenge; a temporal-dynamic algorithm accounting for pathogen-specific detection windows; the "detection-disease disconnect" emphasizing clinical contextualization of NAAT positivity; and multi-analyte integration combining NAAT with viability markers and host inflammatory signatures. We also position these frameworks relative to prior diagnostic-interpretation theories, including STARD, QUADAS-2, MIQE, Bayesian pretest-posttest reasoning, Ct-value interpretation guidance, and host-response classifier frameworks. We compare ten clinically significant pathogens across technical and biological parameters, evaluate point-of-care deployment strategies, and address antimicrobial resistance testing. Performance metrics are presented as context-dependent estimates rather than fixed constants. The next frontier lies not in incremental assay improvements but in system-level integration of pathogen detection, viability assessment, host-response profiling, and clinical phenotyping, supported by artificial intelligence-enhanced interpretation and global standardization efforts.

title: From internal discrimination to external transportability: A multi-layer evaluation of gestational maternal-blood transcriptomic signals associated with later neurodevelopment.
authors: Koc, Sumeyye; Kazanc, Emine; Yusufoglu, Busra
abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal blood transcriptomic profiles during pregnancy may capture biological states associated with later neurodevelopment, but internally detectable signals may not transport across populations, tissues, molecular layers, or experimental systems. We evaluated the internal robustness and cross-context transportability of a pathway-level maternal gestational transcriptomic signal associated with later atypical neurodevelopment. METHODS: Maternal gestational blood transcriptomes from 214 MARBLES pregnancies were summarized using 619 prespecified pathway scores and modeled for atypical versus typical neurodevelopment using repeated nested cross-validation. Internal signal specificity was assessed by repeating the complete discovery procedure after 1000 outcome-label permutations. The resulting pathway findings were then evaluated across independent transcriptomic cohorts, orthogonal methylomic datasets, autism common-variant genetic data, developmental brain atlases, and CRISPR perturbation of neurodevelopmental-risk genes in human neural cells. RESULTS: The discovery procedure achieved an out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.693, PR-AUC of 0.677, and Brier score of 0.227, outperforming all 1000 phenotype-permuted runs of the same pipeline (empirical P = 0.001). Leave-one-batch-out performance was heterogeneous. Independent cord-blood transcriptomics provided limited directional support, whereas placental transcriptomics did not replicate the signal. Methylomic analyses showed limited support, common-variant genetics showed no detectable convergence, and neural CRISPR perturbations showed no functional convergence. Developmental atlas analysis demonstrated strong localization of the fetal inhibitory-interneuron pathway to inhibitory neurons. CONCLUSIONS: The maternal gestational blood signal was internally distinguishable from chance expectations but showed limited transportability across independent biological contexts. These findings distinguish within-cohort molecular predictiveness from broader biological generalizability and support multi-context stress testing before prenatal molecular signals are interpreted as portable biomarkers or mechanisms.

title: Toward detection of heart failure: development of a sensitive fluorescent kit for clinical sST2 detection.
authors: Ping, Zhou; Chen, Menghan; Jin, Yage; Gu, Mengke; Pan, Liang; Zang, Jinzhi; Nai, Shanshan; Song, Ting; Liu, Miaoyuan; Ren, Kaidi; Zhao, Huijie; Yang, Yang
abstract: Heart failure, the terminal stage of various cardiovascular diseases, typically presents with subtle early symptoms that are difficult to detect. Consequently, developing fast and accurate diagnostic tools is essential for effective early diagnosis and disease management. Soluble suppression of tumorigenicity 2 (sST2) is recognized as a valuable biomarker for predicting disease severity and mortality in cardiovascular disease, making it a promising target for developing a detection kit for early heart failure diagnosis. Recently, the CRISPR-Cas12a system has been increasingly used for quick and sensitive nucleic acid detection. However, its application in protein detection remains limited. In this study, we combined nanotechnology-mediated protein capture with the CRISPR-Cas12a system and developed a fluorescence-based method for rapid and sensitive detection of sST2. The presence of sST2 triggers the formation of a ternary complex, which can activate the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, resulting in cleavage of the response DNA single strand and the production of a fluorescent signal. Importantly, when tested on serum samples, this method can effectively distinguish patients with heart failure from healthy controls. This method offers a promising alternative to traditional enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), with potential advantages in operational simplicity and detection speed. Therefore, this innovative fluorescence-based sST2 detection technique has significant potential for the clinical diagnosis of heart failure.

title: Core effectors of the Fusarium pan-effectome contribute to host specificity.
authors: Blackman, Chris T; Aguayo-Limon, Alexia; Lei, Tian; Zarrouki, Malaika; Balcerzak, Margaret; Witte, Thomas; Rampitsch, Christof; Desveaux, Darrell; Subramaniam, Rajagopal
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Fusarium fungi cause economically important diseases of cereal crops, including Fusarium head blight, ear blight, and root rot. Central to these interactions are secreted effector proteins that manipulate host biology to promote infection. In turn, plants have evolved to recognize effector activity to activate immune responses and restrict disease. Despite their importance, the diversity, conservation, and evolution of Fusarium effectors remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Fusarium sambucinum Species complex Effector Compendium (FUSEC), a sequence-defined pan-effectome constructed from 188 high-quality genomes representing 27 species. FUSEC comprises 4,057 sequence-defined effector families, including a conserved soft-core repertoire of 235 families present in at least 95% of isolates. Structure-guided comparisons reorganized these conserved families into 184 structure-defined groups, revealing relationships that extend beyond sequence similarity and identifying similarities to numerous experimentally characterized fungal (a)virulence factors. Despite their broad conservation, soft-core families exhibited substantial within-family sequence diversity, and analyses of diversifying selection identified 44 candidate families undergoing adaptive evolution. Functional screening revealed that the majority of these candidates altered wheat immune responses, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletions in Fusarium graminearum demonstrated that multiple conserved effectors contribute to cultivar-dependent Fusarium head blight severity.

title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies.
authors: Marei, Hany E
abstract: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.

title: AI-enhanced biosensing for antimicrobial resistance: translating rapid diagnostics to global surveillance.
authors: Manisekaran, Nirmal Kumar; Tiwari, Pallavi; Rathinasabapathi, Pasupathi
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates rapid and reliable diagnostic technologies to support timely antimicrobial selection and stewardship. Although conventional culture-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) remains clinically important, its extended turnaround time limits timely intervention, while molecular diagnostics can rapidly identify resistance determinants but may not accurately predict phenotypic resistance. This review critically examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with biomedical microdevices and biosensors for rapid AMR detection, encompassing microfluidic and lab-on-chip platforms, electrochemical and optical biosensors, and CRISPR-based technologies. Emphasis is placed on the application of AI for signal processing, noise reduction, pattern recognition, multiplexed detection, and predictive interpretation of complex biosensor outputs. Key translational challenges, including biofouling, matrix interference, sample-preparation variability, bubble formation, evaporation, signal drift, invalid-test rates, device reproducibility, and inadequate standardisation of reporting and validation, are critically evaluated. The requirements for embedded AI, including memory, computational resources, latency, and energy efficiency, are also considered for portable point-of-care deployment. Analytical, clinical, and operational validation are distinguished, with emphasis on prospective multicentre evaluation using representative specimens and reference AST methods. Beyond clinical diagnosis, AI-enabled microdevices offer potential for decentralised AMR surveillance across wastewater, agricultural, veterinary, and environmental settings within a One Health framework. Translation will require standardised datasets, generalisable and explainable AI, scalable manufacturing, regulatory oversight, data governance, and equitable deployment. Overall, AI-integrated biomedical microdevices represent a promising approach to rapid, decentralised, and actionable AMR diagnostics and surveillance, contingent on robust real-world validation.

title: Engineering collateral cleavage kinetics: a three-state framework for programmable CRISPR-Cas12 molecular transduction.
authors: Verma, Vanshika; Deshmukh, Rehan
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12 nucleic acid diagnostics have achieved very low limits of detection, particularly when coupled to pre-amplification, yet further gains in sensitivity now have limited clinical value compared with the persistent problems of poor reproducibility across samples, matrices, and operators. Existing reviews describe the collateral (trans) cleavage of Cas12 qualitatively (fast turnover, decoupled from target recognition) but offer no common language for comparing platforms or troubleshooting failures. This article proposes a three-state kinetic framework: a conceptual, semi-quantitative scheme that uses four rate constants to classify assay behaviour by regime. It is not a mathematical model for calculating reagent concentrations; the constants serve to identify which step limits performance and give indicative literature ranges for the parameters and their experimental proxies. Using the framework, we assigned the three most frequently reported failure modes (pre-activation leakage, activation delay, and quantitative collapse) to distinct rate-limiting steps and pair each with testable engineering interventions, distinguishing the matrix effects that must be removed by sample preparation from those that should be handled by kinetic design and translate the framework into a decision tree that links deployment setting, output requirement, and sample matrix to a target kinetic regime and transduction interface. A comparison with Cas9 recasts Cas12 from a sensitive nuclease into a kinetically programmable signal generator. Finally, we propose a minimal kinetic reporting set that developers can use to compare assay robustness across studies.

title: Interleukin-6 signaling disrupts blastocyst development and cell lineage composition in cattle.
authors: Pollock, Abigayle B; O'Neill, Hannah C; Oliver, Mary A; Nix, Jada L; Biase, Fernando H; Ealy, Alan D
abstract: The bovine embryo expresses interleukin-6 (IL6) as well as its receptor system, which includes the ligand-binding IL6 receptor subunit (IL6R) and the common IL6 family signal-transducing component (IL6ST). Our laboratory recently determined that IL6ST activity facilitates normal in vitro embryo development and proper inner cell mass (ICM) size and morphology. We therefore hypothesized that embryo-derived IL6, acting through the IL6R-IL6ST receptor complex, drives these developmental outcomes. To test this, two single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting exon 2 of IL6R were designed and electroporated with Cas9 protein into bovine zygotes. Editing efficiency was assessed in 16-cell embryos through targeted IL6R genotyping. Disruption of IL6R did not alter cleavage or development to the 16-cell stage but reduced blastocyst formation on days 7 and 8. The IL6R-edited blastocysts that were generated had reduced ICM cell numbers, no changes in trophectoderm (TE) cell number, and a reduced ICM:TE ratio. In summary, loss of IL6R signaling compromises blastocyst formation and alters cellular composition by reducing ICM cell numbers, thus supporting an embryotrophic role for embryo-derived IL6 acting through the IL6R/IL6ST complex. However, the absence of earlier developmental defects, which occurred in our prior IL6ST-targeting studies, suggests that additional embryo-derived IL6-family cytokines likely also contribute to pre-blastulation development in cattle.

title: Systematic evaluation of 39 testis-enriched genes for male fertility in mice using CRISPR/Cas9.
authors: Tonai, Shingo; Mashiko, Daisuke; Pan, Chen; Chang, Hsin-Yi; Pham, Anh Hoang; Wang, Haoting; Oyama, Yuki; Kitakaze, Hiroaki; Luo, Mengjiao; Sun, Jiang; Castaneda, Julio M; Ishikawa-Yamauchi, Yu; Lu, Yonggang; Shimada, Keisuke; Ikawa, Masahito
abstract: The testis expresses approximately 18,700 genes, more than any other tissue. Among these, 1,262 genes show high and testis-enriched expression, but only a subset is essential for male fertility. Knockout mouse phenotypes provide important information for assessing gene function; however, fertility phenotypes are not always reported, particularly when knockout mice are viable and show no obvious reproductive abnormalities. Reporting such negative fertility phenotypes would help avoid redundant studies and facilitate the prioritization of genes with critical roles in male reproduction. In this study, we generated 38 knockout mouse lines to evaluate the roles of 39 testis-enriched genes in male reproduction using the CRISPR/Cas9 system (1700025B11Rik, 4930444P10Rik, 4930550C14Rik, 4930558K02Rik, 4930590J08Rik, 4933412E24Rik, Acsbg2, Ankmy1, Ankrd61, Apobec4, Arl14epl, Atf7ip2, Ccdc110, Csnka2ip, D11Wsu47e, Ddi1, Efcab8, Fam243, Fam50b, Gm36245, Gtf2a1l, Iqca1l, Litafd, Lrp2bp, Mroh5, Nlrp14, Pebp4, Prss38, Pudp, Slc6a16, Spata1, Spata32, Styxl1, Tcp11, Tcp11x2, Tmem225, Tmem232, Trim52, Trp53tg5). All 38 knockout mouse lines were viable and showed no marked developmental or behavioral abnormalities. We identified 30 fertile KO lines (covering 31 genes) that are dispensable for male fertility under the conditions tested. Reproductive phenotypes for nine of the examined lines had been reported previously; six showed phenotypes consistent with previous reports, whereas three showed discrepant phenotypes. These systematic phenotyping data provide a useful resource for prioritizing candidate genes involved in male fertility and for disseminating both fertility-associated and fertility-unassociated phenotypes to the research community.

title: Inhibition of heat shock protein 90 in the mouse spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception via the upregulation of dual specificity protein phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) in CGRP neurons.
authors: Gabriel, Katherin A; Bowden, Jessica L; Streicher, John M
abstract: In an extended series of studies, we have shown that Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) has a novel role in regulating opioid signal transduction and antinociception in both the brain and spinal cord. Inhibition in the spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception, which led to the finding that an isoform-selective Hsp90 inhibitor could improve opioid therapy, both enhancing pain relief and reducing side effects. However, the signaling mechanisms for this activity are still not fully understood. We thus identified Dual Specificity Phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) from an earlier proteomic study as a protein enhanced in the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibition. Using male and female CD-1 mice, we confirmed that DUSP15 is upregulated in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibitor (17-AAG) treatment. Using CRISPR and siRNA-mediated knockdown, we showed that DUSP15 was necessary for the enhanced morphine antinociception after Hsp90 inhibitor treatment in both the tail flick and post-surgical paw incision pain models. Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and behavioral tools, we placed DUSP15 upstream of both ERK MAPK and AMPK in the opioid signaling cascade. We then used IHC to demonstrate that DUSP15 upregulation occurs at least in part in CGRP neurons, and using cell-selective CRISPR, showed that DUSP15 in CGRP neurons is necessary for the enhanced antinociception observed with spinal Hsp90 inhibitor treatment. Together these studies further expand the known mechanisms by which Hsp90 regulates opioid signal transduction and pain relief and provide basic science insight into a potential strategy to improve opioid therapy using Hsp90 inhibitors.

title: Same hydrolase knockouts, different outcomes: CRISPR/Cas9 editing workflow shapes resulting cellular phenotype and transcriptome in CHO.
authors: Weiss, Linus; Schneider, Stefan; Otte, Kerstin; Fischer, Simon
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9-based multi-gene knockout strategies are widely applied to engineer Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, yet the impact of editing workflow on cellular outcomes remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically compare sequential and multiplex genome editing approaches to generate CHO cell lines lacking nine polysorbate (PS)-degrading hydrolases. Both strategies achieved comparable functional outcomes, markedly improving PS stability. However, they produced distinct phenotypic and transcriptomic trajectories. Sequential editing led to progressive declines in growth and viability, increased cell size and DNA content, and extensive transcriptomic remodeling. In contrast, multiplex editing resulted in milder phenotypic alterations and a substantially smaller transcriptional footprint, albeit with increased clone-to-clone heterogeneity. Transcriptome analyses revealed limited overlap between final states, indicating workflow-specific adaptation despite the same intended knockout set. Importantly, transcriptional changes were primarily associated with clonal selection and iterative manipulation rather than reflecting a shared response to the targeted knockouts themselves. These findings demonstrate that genome editing workflows can shape cellular phenotypes independently of intended genetic modifications. For cell line development, multiplex editing offers a strategy to reduce development time and limit undesirable drift when targeting non-essential genes, highlighting the need to consider engineering strategy as a critical design parameter.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-based Genome Editing in Inherited Diseases: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Advances, Safety and Clinical Translation.
authors: Fatima, Javeria; Siddique, Yasir Hasan
abstract: Gene therapy has transformed modern biomedical research by enabling curative strategies that target the molecular basis of disease. Among genome-editing technologies, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a versatile and efficient platform due to its programmability, simplicity, and precision. This review summarizes the evolution of gene therapy and highlights the therapeutic potential of CRISPR-based genome editing. CRISPR/Cas9 has demonstrated significant potential in correcting disease-causing mutations across multiple inherited disorders, including sickle cell disease, beta- thalassemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, phenylketonuria, muscular dystrophies, and cystic fibrosis. Emerging technologies such as base editing and prime editing further improved editing precision and reduced unintended genomic alterations. However, challenges including off-target effects, DNA repair pathway bias, immune responses, and vector-associated toxicities remain major limitations. The review highlights the rapid progress of CRISPR-mediated therapeutics and emphasizes the importance of improving editing accuracy, delivery efficiency, and long-term safety. Advances in vector engineering and genome-editing platforms are expected to overcome current technical and ethical barriers, facilitating broader clinical applications. CRISPR/Cas9 and related genome- editing technologies represent promising disease-modifying and potentially curative therapeutic approaches. Continued optimization of precision, safety, and delivery systems will be essential for successful translation into routine clinical practice.

title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems.
authors: Brussow, Harald
abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD(+). Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD(+) from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

title: ABCG Transporter Knockouts Alter Integument and Eye Pigmentation With Gene-Specific Effects on Viability in Butterflies and Moths.
authors: Shodja, Donya N; Yan, Joseph; Livraghi, Luca; Yamada, Amika; Harvey-Samuel, Tim; Martin, Arnaud; Mazo-Vargas, Anyi
abstract: Insects possess remarkable diversity in pigmentation across life stages, generated from a limited number of pigment precursors. ABCG transporters play central roles in pigmentation by mediating the intracellular transport of these precursors, yet their functions outside a few model systems remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigate the roles of the ABCG transporter genes white (w), scarlet (st), and oily kinshiryu (ok) across five lepidopteran species representing both butterflies and moths. CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts reveal conserved, tissue-specific functions of ABCG transporters throughout development, affecting larval and pupal integuments as well as adult eyes, but not scale coloration. Notably, our data indicate that both ommochrome and uric acid deposition underlie the coloration and opacity of Lepidoptera larvae and pupae, with the relative contributions of these pathways differing across species and stages. We also reveal that the vivid orange coloration of gulf fritillary caterpillars arises from the interplay of ommochromes and urate granules, providing a clear example of how these pathways combine to produce diverse integument pigmentation. Loss of white was deleterious in four species examined, whereas scarlet knockouts produced viable individuals with easily detectable pigmentation phenotypes, identifying scarlet mutant backgrounds as a practical genetic marker for functional studies. Together, these findings show that conserved ABCG transporter complexes are differentially deployed across tissues and life stages, providing a mechanistic basis for the evolutionary diversification of pigmentation in Lepidoptera and enabling expanded functional genomics and transgenesis in emerging model species.

title: Optix Regulates Abdominal Melanin Pigmentation in the Tobacco Hawkmoth Manduca sexta.
authors: Chatterjee, Martik; Hatto, Gabriel C; Duplais, Christophe; Varnell, Jarrod; Raguso, Robert A; Reed, Robert D
abstract: Research on butterflies has uncovered a conserved "toolkit" of genes for color pattern development and evolution. One of these genes is optix, a homeobox transcription factor that regulates ommochrome and melanin pigmentation, as well as structural coloration, in nymphalid butterflies. It remains unclear, however, whether optix plays any roles in color patterning outside of the Nymphalidae.
