We used CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt optix in the tobacco hornwormmoth Manduca sexta and observed a dramatic abdominal pigmentation phenotype, where orange pigmentation was replaced by black eumelanin. Chemical assays suggest that the orange pigment is not an ommochrome, indicating that optix modulates an alternative, uncharacterized pigment pathway in M. sexta. RNA-seq and chemical analyses of orange and black abdominal scales lead us to speculate that the orange pigment may be a type of melanin, perhaps N-beta-alanyldopamine (NBAD) sclerotin. Our results suggest that optix plays a deeply ancestral role in pigment regulation in Lepidoptera, and demonstrates evolutionary flexibility in how it interfaces with pigment chemistry across moths and butterflies.

title: Generation of transgene-free MtABCG46 mutants in Medicago truncatula using CRISPR/Cas9.
authors: Awasthi, Praveen; Pawela, Aleksandra; Anirudhan, Krishnapriya; Jasinski, Michal
abstract: BACKGROUND: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters form one of the largest and most functionally diverse families of membrane proteins in plants, with members of the ABCG subfamily playing central roles in the transport of specialized metabolites and stress adaptation. In legumes functional analyses of these transporters have been limited by functional redundancy, accessibility of T-DNA inserted mutant lines, and the constraints of RNA interference-based approaches. RESULTS: To address these limitations, we used Medicago truncatula ABCG46 transporter and established hairy root-based CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing platform that enables rapid empirical validation of single guide RNAs prior to stable transformation. Two guide RNAs targeting distinct exons of MtABCG46 were evaluated in 70 independent hairy root lines, revealing strong editing activity for one guide, while the second proved non-functional despite favourable in silico predictions. Sequence analysis identified a range of insertions and deletions, including a homozygous biallelic mutant carrying frame-shifting deletions predicted to abolish transporter function. Using the validated guide RNA, stable Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation yielded heritable mutations, and transgene-free knockout lines were recovered in subsequent generations. CONCLUSIONS: This study establishes a robust hairy root-based gRNA validation platform for M. truncatula, generates stable and heritable mtabcg46 knockout lines, and provides a scalable framework for functional characterization of ABCG transporters in specialized metabolism and plant defense.

title: Identification and functional characterization of the PP2C gene family reveal their negative regulatory roles in stress adaptation in Solanaceae.
authors: Chen, Hong; Yang, Yang; Chen, Dehan; He, Qian; Li, Chengjie; Zhang, Binghui; Chen, Mingjian; Li, Yani; Gu, Gang; Li, Wenqing; Xie, Xiaofang
abstract: BACKGROUND: The plant protein phosphatases 2C (PP2Cs) are key regulators of plant growth and development, hormone signaling, and responses to environmental stresses. In Solanaceae crops, which are frequently challenged by environmental stresses leading to yield losses, a comprehensive cross-species understanding of PP2C family evolution and function remains limited. This study aimed to systematically identify PP2C gene family members in tobacco and eggplant and to perform comparative genomic and functional analyses across representative Solanaceae species, thereby clarifying their evolutionary relationships and stress-responsive roles. RESULTS: In this study, we identified 204 NtPP2C genes in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) and 89 SmPP2C genes in eggplant (Solanum melongena L.). The PP2C genes in both species were unevenly distributed across chromosomes, and segmental duplication appeared to be the major driving force underlying family expansion, with most homologous gene pairs subjected to purifying selection. Phylogenetic analysis classified these PP2C proteins into 12 subgroups (A-L). Members within different subgroups exhibited both conserved and divergent features in conserved motifs, exon-intron organization, and the composition of upstream promoter elements. Analyses of cis-acting elements, protein-protein interaction networks, and gene expression profiles indicated that NtPP2C and SmPP2C genes are broadly involved in light responses, developmental regulation, ABA signaling, drought, cold and heat stress responses, and pathogen infection-related processes. Subcellular localization analysis showed that NtPP2C91 and SmPP2C24, both belonging to the functionally important subgroup A, were localized to the nucleus. Further functional validation showed that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of NtPP2C91 in tobacco and virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of SmPP2C24 in eggplant significantly enhanced plant tolerance to low temperature and resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum (Ras) infection, while modulating the transcriptional dynamics of ABA signaling components and PP2C homologs. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide valuable genetic resources and a theoretical basis for dissecting ABA-mediated stress-resistance regulatory networks in solanaceous crops and offer potential targets for molecular breeding aimed at improving stress tolerance.

title: CDC7 and CDK8 kinases cooperate to support DNA replication origin firing in human cells.
authors: Rainey, Michael D; Bernard, Stefanus; Pravi, Aikaterini; Farrell, Liadhan; Hernandez-Reyes, Yeray; Morrison, Aline M; Boos, Dominik; Ryan, Colm J; Santocanale, Corrado
abstract: The coordinated activation of DNA replication origins is important for efficient DNA synthesis and genome stability. S-phase cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), together with CDC7 kinase, are essential for origin activation by converting the pre-replicative complex into a fully active helicase. Here, in order to identify genes that tune DNA replication, we performed a chemogenetic genome-wide CRISPR-KO screen in cells challenged with the CDC7 inhibitor XL413. By developing a methodology based on genetic co-essentiality to functionally cluster the hits, we uncover the transcriptional CDK8/CCNC kinase in a cluster with replication initiation factors. Depletion of CDK8 further reduces the rate of DNA synthesis imposed by CDC7 inhibitors. DNA fibre experiments further support that CDK8 and CDC7 cooperate in origin activation. Suppression of DNA synthesis by CDK8 inhibition requires the binding of CDK8/CCNC to the MDM2 Binding Protein (MTBP), and we show that CDC7 and CDK8 associate with the MCM complex and individually contribute to the phosphorylation of the replicative helicase. In conclusion, this work adds CDK8 to the list of kinases directly involved in origin activation in human cells.

title: Widening the BRCAness therapeutic window for its synthetic lethality effects with PARP inhibitors.
authors: Fernandez, Anthony; Salman, Yuvika; Castillo, Roxanne; Glackin, Carlotta; Shen, Binghui
abstract: This review examines the expanding role of PARP inhibitors in cancer therapy, moving beyond the traditional model of single-strand break repair inhibition and BRCA-dependent synthetic lethality. We highlight emerging evidence that PARP inhibitors induce cytotoxicity through replication-associated DNA damage, including defects in Okazaki fragment maturation and replication gap accumulation. By integrating recent mechanistic insights with findings from CRISPR-based screens, we outline how disruptions in DNA replication and repair pathways define a broader BRCAness phenotype. We further emphasize the clinical implications of these discoveries, including novel combination strategies that extend the therapeutic applicability of PARP inhibitors beyond prevailing treatment regimens.

title: Reframing decentralized diagnostics with a programmable multi-dimensional microfluidic system.
authors: Xu, Tao; Zhang, Ying; Tang, Xin; Wei, Hongguo; Kang, Lingyan; Zhou, Qize; Li, Shunji; Zhao, Xudong; Li, Jiashuo; Zhang, Zimeng; Wan, Chao; Zhang, Yufei; Chen, Dongjuan; Tian, Ye; Liu, Bi-Feng; Chen, Peng
abstract: Decentralized diagnostics are vital for infectious disease control, yet current point-of-care tools remain largely one-dimensional, failing to capture the multidimensional profiles required for precision management. Here, we show SID-WAVES (Smartphone-Integrated Diagnostics with Wax-encoded Amplified and Versatile Evaluation System), an intelligent, multimodal microfluidic platform. Integrating low-melting-point phase-change and dual-siphon valves with RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a nucleic acid detection and protein immunoassays, the platform enables automated, one-step, sample-to-answer operation via an AI-assisted smartphone readout that reduces operator-dependent variability. Spatial-temporal-signal encoding supports multiplexed, multi-sample, and multimodal analysis, achieving attomolar-level sensitivity (10(-18) M) and >95% diagnostic accuracy across 225 clinical and self-collected molecular assays, demonstrating robust usability. For proteins, a triple-amplification strategy and hierarchical capture enhance sensitivity 125-fold, improving accuracy from 87.6% to 100% in 54 simulated samples. Functioning as a reconfigurable analytical framework where panels are changed by swapping targets and probes, this work helps mitigate the Sensitivity-Multiplexing-Accessibility trade-off, reframing decentralized diagnostics from single-target screening to multi-dimensional health profiling.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR-screening identifies p53 as regulator of cancer cell sensitivity to the histone evicting anthracycline aclarubicin.
authors: van der Zanden, Sabina Y; Schipper, Koen; van Gelder, Merle A; Teunisse, Amina; Sarthy, Jay; Jochemsen, Aart G; Wijdeven, Ruud H M; Neefjes, Jacques
abstract: The anthracycline family, with its prime member doxorubicin, is one of the cornerstones in cancer chemotherapy and acts by poisoning topoisomerase II, resulting in DNA double-stranded breaks. One of its members, aclarubicin, is considered a distinct member of this family due to its inability to inflict DNA double-strand breaks. Despite this, aclarubicin is an effective anti-cancer drug by evicting histones, resulting in chromatin damage. How aclarubicin-induced chromatin damage induces cell death remains largely unknown. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR screen to identify factors regulating sensitivity of cells to aclarubicin and identified p53 as a critical factor for cellular sensitivity. Even though aclarubicin does not induce DNA breaks, treatment resulted in swift activation of ATM independent of the MRN complex, which stabilized and activated p53, resulting in apoptosis and cell cycle arrest. Furthermore, response to aclarubicin treatment could reasonably be predicted by the p53-status of cell lines. These data suggest that ATM and p53 can be activated for apoptosis induction by at least two different pathways, DNA- and chromatin damage. Together, these data suggest p53 could be an important factor to stratify patients for treatment with Aclarubicin.

title: PELOTA at the crossroads of tomato fertility and viral resistance.
authors: Singh, Zeenu; Sufrin Ringwald, Tali; Dahan, Yardena; Gelbart, Dana; Kunta, Srinivas; Avni, Ben; Wasserstrom, Haggai; Citovsky, Vitaly; Lapidot, Moshe; Burko, Yogev
abstract: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a major threat to tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) production, and durable resistance remains challenging to achieve. We show that complete loss of function of PELOTA (PELO), a conserved ribosome surveillance factor underlying the resistance allele ty-5, confers near-immunity to TYLCV. Unexpectedly, PELO is also required for reproductive development; pelo mutants display severe floral defects, impaired male and female fertility, and complete sterility, revealing a previously unknown role for PELO in tomato plant fertility. Using CRISPR-mediated promoter editing, we generated novel PELO alleles with reduced expression that maintain fertility while conferring enhanced resistance to TYLCV, providing a new strategy.

title: A History of Cancer Research: Mouse Models of Cancer Genetics.
authors: Lipsick, Joseph
journal: Cold Spring Harbor perspectives in medicine
abstract: Studies of genetically engineered mice have contributed significantly to our understanding of tumor biology, and there are now countless mouse models of different human cancers. Breeding of mice for cancer research began more than 100 years ago. This provided early insights into cancer genetics, but it was the development of techniques for generating transgenic and knockout mice that transformed the field in the 1980s. The advent of CRISPR-Cas technology 30 years later made mouse models even easier to generate. In this excerpt from his forthcoming book on the history of cancer research, Joe Lipsick looks back at a century of advances in mouse cancer genetics, from the early pioneering work of Abbie Lanthrop to the Nobel-winning discoveries that now allow researchers to manipulate potential cancer genes in mice and explore their roles in tumorigenesis.

title: The weight of memory: nutrition, diabetes, and the brain.
authors: Kattner, Aila Akosua
abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA.
authors: Wang, Xiwei; Wu, Yuqi; Zhang, Xinyu; Du, Yingzhen; Liu, Nan; Wang, Zengming; Zhang, Hui; Gao, Xiuli; Zheng, Aiping
abstract: Long single-stranded DNA (long ssDNA) plays important roles in cutting-edge fields such as DNA origami, gene therapy, and synthetic biology. However, the production, preparation, and purification of long ssDNA remain technically challenging. This review systematically summarizes current strategies for long ssDNA production and preparation, including phage-E. coli-based biological production, template-dependent enzymatic amplification, and viral-vector-based generation of ssDNA genomes. CRISPR-Cas-assisted approaches are discussed separately as complementary tools for post-synthetic processing, sequence-selective cleavage, enrichment, and quality control, whereas other enzymatic approaches are considered for post-synthetic strand conversion. We compare the characteristics and limitations of these production and preparation strategies, discuss purification techniques for long ssDNA, and summarize its applications in DNA origami nanotechnology and gene therapy. This review comprehensively synthesizes the bottlenecks in long ssDNA production, preparation, and purification, and outlines further development trends. We highlight template-independent de novo enzymatic DNA synthesis, automated DNA manufacturing, synthetic biology-based production systems, and AI-assisted sequence optimization. These developments are expected to accelerate the transition of long ssDNA technologies from laboratory research toward scalable manufacturing and practical applications.

title: Activating death receptor 5 exposes a cancer cell vulnerability to natural killer and T cell attack.
authors: Chen, Zhen; Raffi, Gabriele Casagrande; Zhao, Ziji; Yang, Chaopin; Chen, Jian; Feng, Xuezhao; Chen, Yanxing; Steur, Marit; Morandi, Pietro; Lieftink, Cor; Lu, Siyi; Xie, Huamei; Zhong, Haoran; Wang, Jing; Willemsen, Lisa; Horlings, Hugo; Beijersbergen, Roderick; Dijkstra, Krijn K; Gao, Song; Xue, Ruidong; Bernards, Rene; Wang, Liqin
journal: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao
abstract: Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer care, yet resistance frequently undermines its efficacy. Although tumor-intrinsic resistance pathways have been mapped, how immune pressure regulates death-receptor vulnerability and anti-apoptotic buffering remains less defined. Using genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening in cancer cells co-cultured with natural killer (NK) cells, we identify CFLAR, encoding cFLIP, as a dominant suppressor of death-receptor signaling that impairs NK- and T-cell cytotoxicity. CFLAR depletion sensitizes cancer cells to NK- and T-cell attack in vitro and in vivo. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses link high CFLAR expression to reduced lymphocyte infiltration and poorer responses to immune checkpoint blockade. Mechanistically, immune effector cell-induced inflammation increases CFLAR and death receptor 5 (DR5) expression in association with p38-MAPK signaling, balancing survival and death under immune pressure. The DR5 agonist conatumumab enhances lymphocyte-mediated killing and improves responses to cellular therapies, checkpoint blockade, and chemo-immunotherapy. Combining DR5 agonism with NKG2A blockade co-activates NK- and T-cell responses and overcomes anti-PD-1 resistance in MHC-I-deficient tumors. These findings identify the DR5-cFLIP axis as an immune-pressure-associated, pharmacologically targetable vulnerability and support rational combinations of DR5 agonists with multiple immunotherapies for refractory cancers.

title: Breast cancer cellular and gene-based therapies: Current approaches, clinical results, and future perspectives.
authors: Donmez, Hulya
abstract: Cellular and gene-based therapies are being investigated as potential strategies to address current treatment limitations in breast cancer. Adoptive cell therapies, such as CAR-T, TCR-T, TILs and NK cell-based therapies, are currently under investigation for their ability to selectively target tumor-associated antigens. Also, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing is being investigated as a strategy to enhance T cell persistence, improve tumor infiltration, and increase resistance to immunosuppressive signaling. Although cellular and gene-based therapies have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, their application in breast cancer remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, immune exclusion, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Among current approaches, TIL-based therapies have provided some of the clearest evidence of clinical activity selected patients, whereas the clinical efficacy of CAR-T and gene-editing strategies as standalone interventions remains uncertain. Future progress may depend on biomarker-guided, combinatorial approaches rather than single-modality therapies. This review examines the current applications, clinical evidence, and limitations of these approaches in breast cancer.

title: Deep CRISPR mutagenesis predicts cancer risk in Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
authors: Penkert, Judith; Grosshennig, Anika; Dutzmann, Christina M; Ewert, Annika; Zimmer, Rika; Schoene-Bake, Jan-Christoph; Moersch, Valentina; Silchmuller, Farina; Gieseke, Josephine; Sanger, Birte; Gerasimov, Tanja; Kratz, Christian P

title: Molecular insights into the long terminal repeat regions of therapeutic staphylococcal Twortvirinae phages.
authors: Amankwah, Stephen; Wicke, Laura; Kaluski, Lukasz; Stefanczyk, Emil; Lobocka, Malgorzata
abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

title: A background-suppressed CRISPR/Cas13a-HRCA biosensor for ultrasensitive miR-137 detection toward differential screening of Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Song, Juan; Yue, Huixin; Zhang, Chuansong; Jiao, Jianwei; Jiao, Jin
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with pathological changes that can occur years before the onset of clinical symptoms, highlighting the importance of sensitive biomarker detection for early diagnosis. Here, we developed a fluorescence biosensing platform based on CRISPR/Cas13a-assisted hyperbranched rolling circle amplification (CRISPR/Cas13a-HRCA) for the detection of the AD-related biomarker miR-137. A duplex composed of Linear-Bio and a Cas13a linker strand was first immobilized on streptavidin-coated magnetic beads to construct magnetic probes. In the presence of miR-137, the linker strand was displaced and released into solution through strand exchange and magnetic separation. The released linker activated the CRISPR/Cas13a system via complementary pairing with crRNA, leading to cleavage of the UUU site within the topological DNA reporter (TDR). The cleaved TDR subsequently initiated the HRCA reaction in the presence of Vent DNA polymerase and the P2 probe, generating abundant double-stranded DNA products for fluorescence readout using SYBR Green I. By combining CRISPR/Cas13a amplification, magnetic separation, and label-free fluorescence detection, the platform produced a fluorescence response to miR-137 over 10 fM-100 nM, with an LOD and LOQ of 1.77 and 11.11 fM, respectively. Recoveries ranged from 99% to 106%, with RSDs of 2.2-2.6% in aCSF. Furthermore, the method successfully distinguished cerebrospinal fluid samples from AD patients and healthy individuals, demonstrating its potential for AD-related miRNA analysis.

title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
authors: Wright, Rosanna C T; Lovell, Simon C; Richmond, Anna; Harrison, Christian; Ashworth, Eleri; Kadioglu, Aras; Fothergill, Joanne L; Friman, Ville-Petri; Westra, Edze R; Brockhurst, Michael A
abstract: Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation. The supply of resistance mutations differed strongly between very closely related lipopolysaccharide-binding phages and was associated with variation at the C-terminus of the tail fibre protein altering residues involved in hydrogen bonding and the predicted binding site. Our results show that CRISPR immunity is more beneficial against virulent phages that are harder to evolve resistance to via receptor mutations, suggesting that virulent phage community composition and diversity will be important drivers of the prevalence of CRISPR immunity.

title: Protocol for comprehensive genotyping of nuclease, base, and prime editing outcomes using CleanFinder.
authors: Dobner, Jochen; Ramachandran, Haribaskar; Rossi, Andrea
abstract: Genome editing experiments often produce heterogeneous allele mixtures that require structured genotyping. Here, we present a protocol for analyzing amplicon sequencing data from nuclease, base, prime, and mitochondrial base editing experiments using CleanFinder. We describe steps for preparing reference sequences and FASTQ files and running browser-native or command-line analyses. We then detail interpretation of genotype distributions, repair signatures, editing efficiencies, and allelic dropout. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Ramachandran et al.(1) and cleanfinder.org.

title: Protocol for engineering primary human and mouse T cells using peptide-assisted genome editing.
authors: Wang, Jianong; He, Yifan; Zhang, Zhen
abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.(1).

title: SFRP2 Editing Enhances Dermal Papilla Cell Function via Activation of the PI3K-Akt Signaling Pathway.
authors: Cai, Jiawei; Fan, Aoyun; Bai, Ziyang; Zhao, Bohao; Chen, Yang; Wu, Xinsheng
abstract: Secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2) is an important molecule that regulates cell growth and development and participates in hair follicle (HF) development and homeostasis. The present study seeks to determine whether SFRP2 directly targets dermal papilla cells (DPCs), the pivotal functional cell population within HF, and characterize the intracellular signaling regulatory network triggered downstream. In this study, a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SFRP2 gene editing DPC model was established in vitro. Multi-omics analyses, including transcriptomics and metabolomics, were performed alongside functional assays to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of SFRP2 in DPCs. Among three designed single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), sgRNA3 showed the highest editing efficiency (67.0%) without off-target effects. Genetic editing of SFRP2 markedly increased the transcript levels of pivotal hair follicle‑development‑related genes (LEF1, CCND1 and Wnt2). Meanwhile, it suppressed TGF‑beta1 transcription, which resulted in elevated proliferation capacity and diminished apoptotic activity within DPCs. Transcriptomic profiling identified 2288 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in PI3K-Akt, MAPK and TNF signaling pathways, while metabolomic analysis identified 185 differential metabolites (DMs) associated with apoptosis, ABC transporters, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Integrated multi-omics analysis confirmed PI3K-Akt signaling as a central regulatory axis. Western blot analysis revealed increased phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt following SFRP2 editing, indicating pathway activation. Treatment of SFRP2-edited DPCs with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduced the elevated phosphorylation and reversed the functional phenotypes, confirming PI3K-Akt pathway involvement. Collectively, these findings indicate that SFRP2 mediates DPC biological activities by means of PI3K‑Akt‑driven transcriptional‑metabolic networks, yielding novel perspectives on the molecular regulatory machinery controlling HF physiology.

title: mV2G: a multiomic atlas for tissue-specific variant-to-gene prioritization.
authors: Zhang, Dean Y; Zhou, Hufeng; Sheth, Maya U; Gschwind, Andreas R; Engreitz, Jesse M; Lin, Xihong; Liu, Hongbo
abstract: The multiomic Variant-to-Gene (mV2G; https://mv2g.hbliulab.org) is a comprehensive atlas that integrates diverse functional genomic evidence to prioritize tissue-specific variant-to-gene (V2G) associations. While genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified millions of associations between genetic variants and diseases, translating these findings into biological mechanisms remains challenging because >90% of variants reside in noncoding regions. Existing V2G resources provide complementary regulatory evidence but are fragmented and often lack tissue-specific interpretation. To address this challenge, we constructed the mV2G atlas by integrating 24 types of functional genomic evidence across 50 human tissues, including molecular quantitative trait loci, enhancer-gene predictions, 3D chromatin interactions, and experimental validation. The atlas contains 188 634 118 evidence-supported V2G pairs involving 13 618 039 variants and 69 521 genes. To prioritize high-confidence V2G pairs, we developed a CRISPR-informed, evidence-weighted model. Using this model, we prioritized 3 348 174 high-confidence V2G pairs, 88% of which were tissue-specific. The mV2G atlas provides searchable variant- and gene-centered interfaces, an interactive browser for visualizing variants, target genes, cis-regulatory elements, and chromatin states, as well as downloadable datasets. By integrating complementary regulatory evidence into a unified framework, mV2G provides an accessible resource for interpreting the functional and phenotypic impact of genomic variation in relevant tissues for human diseases.

title: Map-based cloning and functional validation of Xa50, a wall-associated kinase gene conferring broad-spectrum bacterial blight resistance in rice.
authors: Zhang, Meng; Yuan, Meng
journal: Molecular breeding : new strategies in plant improvement
abstract: Genetically validated broad-spectrum resistance genes are needed to improve bacterial blight resistance breeding in rice. Here, we identified HP178 as a rice accession showing broad-spectrum resistance to geographically diverse Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo) strains and mapped a dominant locus to a 140-kb interval on chromosome 11. Within the mapped interval of the R498 reference genome, annotation and domain analysis identified OsR498G1120741700, which encodes a predicted wall-associated kinase (WAK), as the most likely candidate gene. Genetic complementation in the susceptible cultivar Zhonghua 11 and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in HP178 confirmed that OsR498G1120741700 contributes to the resistance phenotype. The largely overlapping mapping intervals and the correspondence of this gene to ORF5, one of the candidates previously proposed for Xa50(t) in CX315, suggest a possible relationship between the two resistance loci. We therefore tentatively adopt the designation Xa50 to refer to the gene identified here, although its relationship to Xa50(t) in CX315 requires further investigation. Natural-variation analysis of 3,970 rice accessions showed that 936 were classified as Xa50-like, including 443 accessions with the resistance-associated Hap1 haplotype. Functional tests showed that the K435N lines exhibited partially attenuated Xa50-mediated resistance, whereas lines carrying a Hap4-type kinase-domain variant showed severely compromised resistance and reduced ROS accumulation. Our results identify Xa50 as a WAK-type resistance gene and provide haplotype information to support the selection of resistance-associatedXa50 alleles in rice breeding. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-026-01739-5.

title: The SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module integrates gibberellin metabolism to promote plant height in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum).
authors: Zhang, Xingxing; Chai, Miao; Cao, Linjing; Chen, Shengbo; Zhao, Kun; Han, Jiazhen; Li, Ning; Zhao, Hongjiao; Feng, Shengjun; Wang, Bo; Zhang, Shengze; Li, Yumeng; Xu, Mingze; Ren, Guodong; Gao, Shuai
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
abstract: Plant height is an essential agronomic trait that significantly influences crop yield and quality. The HYPONASTIC LEAVES 1 (HYL1), a core component of microRNA biogenesis, remains poorly understood in terms of its regulatory mechanisms on agronomic traits in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Sl). In this study, we demonstrated that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of SlHYL1 caused dwarfism, and partial suppression of SlHYL1 in tomato cultivar "Ailsa Craig" (AC) via RNA interference (RNAi) increased internode number but reduced internode length, resulting in a semi-dwarf phenotype, confirming the role of SlHYL1 in regulating plant height. Cytological analysis showed that SlHYL1 suppression decreased both cell number and size within internodes. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified that SlHYL1 interacted with another tomato RNA-binding protein 1 (SlRBP1). Knockdown of SlRBP1 resembled the SlHYL1-RNAi semi-dwarf phenotype. Further studies revealed that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module additively promotes the expression of gibberellin (GA) biosynthetic genes, thereby facilitating GA accumulation. Additionally, the dwarf phenotypes of both SlHYL1-RNAi and SlRBP1-RNAi plants were partially rescued by exogenous GA(3) application. Notably, unlike SlHYL1, SlRBP1 did not affect the biogenesis of most miRNAs. In summary, our findings demonstrate that the SlHYL1-SlRBP1 module regulates tomato plant height by enhancing GA accumulation.

title: ABCA1 deficiency exacerbates diet-induced atherosclerosis and hepatic xanthomatosis in knockout hamsters.
authors: Chen, Jianwen; Zhang, Wei; Shi, Sijing; Wang, Yuhui; Fan, Jianglin; Yang, Xiawen
abstract: ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) is a critical transmembrane protein that mediates the cellular efflux of cholesterol and phospholipids to extracellular acceptors. Lipid metabolism dysfunctions caused by ABCA1 deficiency in humans have been closely linked to atherosclerotic disease. However, ABCA1 deficient mouse models reported so far are inadequate for faithfully recapitulating the characteristics of dyslipidemia and atherosclerotic pathology seen in ABCA1 deficient patients. To overcome this problem, we attempted to use a golden Syrian hamster model because of its lipid metabolism similarities to humans, and generated ABCA1 knockout (KO) hamsters using the CRISPR/Cas9 technique and examined the pathophysiological consequences of ABCA1 deficiency. On a normal chow diet, ABCA1 KO hamsters exhibited significantly lower levels of plasma total cholesterol (TC) but higher levels of plasma triglycerides (TG) compared with the wild-type (WT) controls. Nevertheless, plasma HDLs were nearly undetectable in KO hamsters. On a high-cholesterol high-fat diet, male KO hamsters displayed more pronounced hyperlipidemia with increased levels of plasma TC and TG compared with those in WT controls, a change attributable to a remarkable increase in TC contents in VLDLs and in TG contents in all apoB-containing lipoproteins, whereas cholesterol in IDLs and large LDLs was reduced. Female KO hamsters, in contrast, showed consistently lower plasma TC levels than WT controls. Pathological analysis showed that ABCA1 deficiency not only promoted aortic atherosclerosis but also caused massive hepatic xanthomatosis in KO hamsters. These results indicate that ABCA1 KO hamsters may become a useful model for the study of human dyslipidemia and atherosclerosis.

title: The Pkd2 gene regulates reproduction and mediates temperature stress tolerance in the oriental fruit fly, Bactrocera dorsalis.
authors: Su, Hong-Ai; Wang, Jia-Rui; Lai, Jia-Yu; Yu, Hai-Kuo; Qi, Yi-Xiang; Lu, Yong-Yue
abstract: BACKGROUND: Most insect species possess either a single TRP-polycystin 2 (TRPP2/Pkd2) gene or lack it entirely. In contrast, the family Tephritidae uniquely possesses two Pkd2 members whose functional roles remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the physiological functions of Pkd2-1 and Pkd2-2 in the tephritid pest Bactrocera dorsalis using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout. RESULTS: Homozygous knockout lines for BdorPkd2-1 and BdorPkd2-2 were generated from wild-type (WT) flies using the CRISPR/Cas9 system. Eggs from BdorPkd2-1 knockout mutants failed to undergo normal embryonic development, resulting in a 0% hatch rate. In contrast, deletion of BdorPkd2-2 significantly reduced the adult mating rate, fecundity, and egg hatchability. Compared with WT flies, BdorPkd2-2(-/-) mutants exhibited shorter heat-knockdown times and longer chill-coma recovery times. Furthermore, adult survival rates for BdorPkd2-2(-/-) mutants were significantly reduced under normal and extreme temperatures. CONCLUSION: BdorPkd2-1 is essential for embryonic development, whereas BdorPkd2-2 plays a critical role in reproduction and thermal stress tolerance in B. dorsalis. These findings advance our understanding of Pkd2 function in tephritid pests and suggest novel strategies for pest control by targeting reproduction or stress responses. title: Rapid RPA-Cas12a Assay for Streptococcus agalactiae Serotype III in Fish Featuring Photocontrolled One-Pot Detection.
authors: Chaijarasphong, Thawatchai; Aiamsa-At, Praphutson; Wongworachart, Sorawit; Senapin, Saengchan
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae is a primary pathogen responsible for significant mortality in tilapia, a critical and affordable source of animal protein. Among the various serotypes affecting aquaculture, serotype III is increasingly recognized for its high virulence and zoonotic potential, with multidrug resistance reported in some lineages. However, diagnostic tools that combine serotype-level resolution with field-deployability remain scarce. In this study, we developed a rapid and specific CRISPR-based detection platform targeting the cpsH gene of S. agalactiae serotype III. Combining recombinase polymerase amplification and CRISPR detection, the standard two-step RPA-Cas12a assay achieved a limit of detection (LoD) of 100 copies per reaction, with no cross-reactivity observed against closely related cpsH homologues from serotypes Ia, Ib and VI. The entire workflow can be completed within 1 h at a constant temperature of 37 degrees C, providing visual readouts that can be easily and unambiguously interpreted. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the assay can be streamlined into a photocontrolled one-pot format, which reduces the risk of aerosol contamination while maintaining the same sensitivity as the two-step protocol. When evaluated against simulated DNA-spiked samples and field samples, both assay formats exhibited 100% concordance with each other and with the conventional PCR method, highlighting the potential of this platform as a step toward rapid, serotype-specific surveillance in aquaculture.

title: Synthetic lethal screens reveal p300/CBP as a vulnerability for GNAQ-driven uveal melanomas.
authors: Zhang, Gui-Ming; Yuan, Junling; Chen, Liang; Jin, Xuan-Yu; Ren, Zhong-Lu; Zhou, Yan-Ling; Zhou, Runhua; Xiao, Ya-Fei; Wang, Jing-Wei; Zhang, Xi-An; Bai, Chongzhi; Li, Zhijie; Li, Yi-Lei; Yu, Le
abstract: Uveal melanoma is the most common intraocular cancer in adults, driven by activating mutations in GNAQ or GNA11, which encode the G proteins Galphaq and Galpha11. Currently, therapeutic options for uveal melanoma, particularly metastatic uveal melanoma, remain limited. Through an isogenic CRISPR screening approach, we identify EP300, which encodes the protein lysine acetyltransferase p300, as a top synthetic lethal vulnerability in the context of GNAQ mutation. Notably, CREBBP, which encodes the closely related paralogue CBP, also emerges among the top-ranked candidates. Mechanistically, we find that p300 and CBP support YAP-dependent transcription downstream of oncogenic Galphaq in uveal melanoma through interactions with YAP at chromatin. These interactions enhance H3K27 acetylation at the promoters and putative enhancers of YAP target genes and promote the recruitment of RNA polymerase II and CDK9. Using multiple in vivo models representing clinically relevant stages of Galphaq-mutant uveal melanoma, we find that p300 inhibition, by both genetic and pharmacological approaches, profoundly impairs tumor growth and metastasis. Taken together, this study establishes p300 as a potential therapeutic target for Galphaq-driven uveal melanoma, which is dependent on unrestrained YAP signaling.
